  • The overview above the fold; art direction (67a) beside it. Not re-measured since the walk of 6 September.
Binding · turn 63 The world overview carries the whole world · the hero loses its controls, and the page goes on to say what the world is made of, what it has been made into, and what is waiting (supersedes 1c; retires the key-art clause of 61a)

Binding. The world overview holds no controls over the world’s pictures. The hero is a name, a logline and a cast — a way in, not a workbench — so the key-art row (Generate key art from the logline, Upload an image, a model picker and the keep-or-discard offer) leaves it, and with it the clause in 61a that put key art here because "the image it feeds is the thing on screen". It is not: the thing on screen is the world. Removing the row leaves the world’s key art with no setter at all, which is a hole to close deliberately rather than by leaving four buttons under a title — see Try next.

Binding. Everything below the fold is derived and clickable, and every figure states what is outstanding beneath it. The glance is four figures over one hairline-divided box — counts of the world’s own entities, never a production’s guests — and each carries a second line naming what is unsettled about that count (N proposed changes, N waiting for approval, N still a sketch), falling back to a settled statement rather than to nothing — the line is pinned at 15px and clipped, so four cells hold one height whatever the world has in it. The figures are figures, not buttons: the tab row above is how those screens are reached, and a second set of doors to the same seven places would be the inventory this page has twice been cleared of.

Binding. Bands on the production tile are pinned — frame 128, format 13, title 19, foot 15 — and the title and foot are clipped to one line each, so three productions with a one-word title, a logline and no shots at all still sit level. A percentage is shown only where shots exist to divide; a story production carries its scene and chapter counts and no bar, because a completion figure over nothing countable is invented. The row takes as many columns as there are productions, to a maximum of three and a minimum of two — two productions are two halves, never two thirds and a hole, and one is never a card the width of the page with a 128px frame in it.

Binding. What needs a person is one line at the foot of the page, or it is absent. It names at most two things — a staged proposal, an open canon thread — each as subject · what kind of decision with the verb that settles it, and it never renders at zero. Only the subject clips: the kind and the verb are flex:none, because a proposal’s summary is a whole sentence and leaving the kind after it in one clipped run made the one thing this line exists to say the first thing the ellipsis ate. This is the narrow re-entry of what turn 44 pulled off this page: the panels that stacked here were screens' worth of content pushing the world’s own entrances below the fold, whereas one line beneath the productions costs nothing above it. The chrome’s warning dot remains the guarantee of findability — this line is a convenience, so it may be capped at two and may sit off-screen without anything being lost.

built · driftedwhat shipped
  • The rack ships. The rail's marks stay hidden until it folds; Audio and Exports in the rail redirect into the Cut; there is no Cast row (production.tsx, fidelity.css).
Binding · turn 120 The season is a rack of frames, the rail is its episode tree, and Arke is an edge — an episode is drawn at the shape it will be watched in, an empty one is an unexposed frame, and the assistant is reachable from every page in the production rather than five of them (redraws 99c and 99d; the rail read off the build, then corrected where it disagrees with turns 93 and 101)

Binding. An episode is drawn as its frame, at 9:16. A microdrama is vertical video and its episodes were drawn as seven bordered paragraphs — a board that would read the same for a podcast. The tile is now the episode’s hook frame at the format’s own aspect ratio, and the hook is set on it rather than beside it, because hook in 3s is what the first frame is for. Seven of them in one row is the season’s shape at a glance — turn 87’s rule, kept, and now visible from across the room.

Binding. An unwritten episode is an unexposed frame, not a dashed box. A dashed card reads as something broken; a blank frame at the same size as a filled one reads as something waiting. The number is the whole of it — no caption, no OPEN TO START IT, which was four copies of an instruction that turn 92 already made unnecessary by fixing every tile to one destination. A staged episode is an unexposed frame in amber, carrying the mark at the point it was pressed, which is turn 92’s other rule.

Binding. The media is the only colour on the page. Chrome, rail, header and panel stay on the neutral ramp; the frames carry the world. This is why the pill row went: six identical outlined chips of 7 episodes, 3 written, 14 scenes repeated what the rail and the meter already count. What survives is a seven-segment meter in the header, in episode order, filled for written and amber for staged — the rack’s own shape at header size.

Binding. Every glyph names a state or a count. The rail carried eight bare words and a gap:9px left for icons nobody drew; it now carries them. Nothing decorative is added: there is no play control on an episode, because Bell Watch has 0 takes and 0:00 cut, and a button that cannot play anything is a lie drawn in the most prominent place on the tile.

Binding. The foot of the season is its cast. Seven frames in one row cannot fill the page and the remainder was white; what belongs in it is the other half of the answer to what is this season, at the same altitude — four faces, named, with the line each was written from. It is not the dashboard returning: turn 93 removed awaiting review and next uncovered shot because they are shot-level, and a season’s cast is not. Episodes at the top of the page, the people at the foot, at every width.

Binding. The rail’s first item is Episodes, and there is nothing above it. Turn 93 bound one entry for the front page; 99c/99d were drawn afterwards still carrying Dashboard, and the build carries Overview and Episodes as two entries that render the same component — the production index and /season both resolve to the season board. Two rows, one screen, is the same failure turn 93 named. It is Episodes, not Season: it is what the rail counts, and turn 99 already settled that a season is its episodes.

Binding. The rail is the episode tree, and the tree is the way to a scene. The build already draws it and the drawing did not: each episode a disclosure carrying its scene count, its scenes beneath it with a state dot, New scene inside the episode it would belong to and New episode under the last. This is why the board has no Scenes entry and needs none — the rack chooses an episode, the tree chooses a scene, and neither repeats the other.

Binding. Every destination has a mark, and no two share one. Turn 101 bound the first half and the build keeps it; the second half is broken in two places. Folded, the mark is the item — and Takes and Cut are drawn with the same glyph, as are Story structure and Artifacts. Two pairs of identical rows in the one state where the labels are gone. Takes takes the stack (attempts at one shot) and Story structure takes the branch (arcs across a season); Cut keeps the camera and Artifacts the folder.

Binding. The marks are shown expanded as well as folded. Today they are display:none until the rail folds, so the only state that shows a mark is the state that has taken the word away: nobody ever learns which glyph is Cut before they need to read the rail by glyph alone. Showing the mark beside its label costs a column of 15px and is what teaches the folded rail — 120d is only legible because 120a was.

Binding. Audio and Exports sit with the Cut, because that is where they open. Both are lenses on the editor rather than screens (SPEC-039 R-1, T-5: the addresses resolve to cut?library=audio and cut?export=1), and the build lists Audio two rows above the thing it opens. A rail’s order is a claim about what is near what. Cast returns to the episodic rail in the same group: SPEC-020 R-9 puts it on every format’s rail and the episodic branch is the one that dropped it, which leaves a production’s own guests reachable only by a link on a page — and not at all once the rail folds.

Binding. Arke is an edge of the production, not a feature of five screens. The panel docks against the right edge of the production frame, so the way to it is the same on every page in the production — the Cut, Generate, Cast, Exports, the season, an episode, a scene. Today it is built on five screens and reachable on no others, which makes it a thing that appears rather than a thing that is there. A control a person has to hunt for by route is one they stop looking for.

Binding. Put away, Arke is the strip — and the strip is the one the scene already draws. 42px of --muted against the frame’s right edge: a filled dot, Ask Arke set vertically, and the pin at the foot. This is not a new control. The scene workspace built it (.fy-sw__rail, SPEC-036) and it is lifted to the layout unchanged, because somebody who learned the affordance on a scene must not meet a different one on the Cut. Pressing it docks the panel; the panel’s pin returns it to the strip. Two states, 42px and 330px, and the strip never disappears.

Binding. The pin always exists, and being docked is the person’s decision, not the route’s. onPutAway is optional in the build and the season and the episode both omit it, so on the two screens this turn draws the panel cannot be dismissed at all — 330px of a 1360px frame that the person has no way to reclaim. It is required. And the answer holds across the production the way the rail’s fold does (turn 101): walking season — Cut — season must not put Arke back and take it away again.

Binding. The right edge is one pane, and the strip is its closed state. Arke is reached three different ways today. On the season and the episode it is simply there and cannot be dismissed. On a scene it is the panel and its strip. On the Cut it is a tab — an Inspector | Arke pair in a side pane, opened by a toolbar button whose label changes to name whichever tab was last used, so the control reads Inspector on the day you want Arke and cannot be learned. One closed state everywhere: the strip. What the pane holds when it opens is the page’s business — on the Cut, Inspector and Arke as tabs, because the editor genuinely has two things to show beside a timeline; on the season, Arke alone and no tab strip, which turn 91 already called a heading wearing a border. The strip always opens Arke, and the Inspector keeps a control of its own with a fixed name.

Binding. The strip carries no subject; the panel does. Turn 99 bound the subject into the panel’s header, and one control on every page means the subject changes with the route — the season here, the cut there. The strip says only that Arke is here: there is room for one word in 42px, and a strip that named its subject would be a second, quieter header arguing with the page’s own. The subject appears the moment it docks.

Binding. What the panel costs is said. With Arke docked the rack keeps all seven frames and loses the hook overlay and the cliff line (120b): at 93px a frame cannot hold a readable sentence, and shrinking the type to fit is how a board becomes unreadable in both states instead of one. The number, the title and the state survive at every width, which is what the screen is for; the hook and the cliff are on the episode’s own page either way.

  • Shipped by PR 1039: the world's shelf and this production's own in one grid, only here on the card.
Binding · turn 134 The production’s artifacts — a page inside the production that holds the world’s shelf and its own, instead of a rail row that leaves (amends 120 and 68a)

Binding. The rail row stays inside the production. Artifacts addresses /w/<world>/p/<production>/artifacts, under the production layout, so the rail, the crumb and the back door are unchanged by pressing it. No row on a production rail may address a world route. Its count is what its own page shows — the world’s shelf plus this production’s own — and never one scope’s number over another scope’s destination.

Binding. Every production has the row, above Generate. 120 drew Artifacts on the season rail only, and the build put it there only. A film, a music video, an interactive video and a novel all file references, recordings and documents, so the row sits after the divider and directly above Generate on every format’s rail. On the episodic rail that leaves Takes · Artifacts · Generate · Cut unchanged; on every other video rail it is a new row reading Artifacts · Generate · Cut. A novel has neither of those, so there it opens the same group under its own divider and is the last row: the rule is after the divider, at the head of the trailing group, and above Generate is what that means wherever a Generate exists.

Binding. One grid, and ownership is a word on the card. The world’s shelf and this production’s own are one set in one grid — the set every picker and the Cut’s Library already work from — ordered together and never split into bands. A file this production owns leads its meta line with only here, set in the foreground so a mixed grid reads without reaching for the chips; a world file says nothing, because on the world’s own shelf there would be nothing to say. Three ownership chips lead the filter row, All, Only here and From the world, before the kind chips and Made here. Another production’s files are never in the set, and the page does not mention them.

Binding. Add files files into this production. Both entrances — the door press and the dashed cell at the end of the grid — scope what they take to this production, and the cell says so where the file will appear: only in <production> · up to 16 at a time. Nothing on this page files to the world; the world’s shelf keeps its own unscoped press. Under the From the world lens the dashed cell is absent, because there is nothing this page can add there.

Binding. What changes the world happens on the world’s shelf. Remove and Lift facts are offered on a file this production owns and on no other. A world artifact is read, opened, placed and cited from here; it is retired and extracted where it lives. This keeps SPEC-020 R-12 honest without a caveat on the page — a production-scoped document lifts guests and never canon, and a world document is never lifted from a production. Retired is a lens on this production’s own retirements only, which is the same rule read backwards: you can restore here exactly what you could remove here.

Binding. The Cast screen stops holding files. The FILED HERE · ONLY IN <PRODUCTION> list at the foot of Cast is retired with this page; guests are Cast’s subject and a production’s recordings and documents are not. Cast keeps its guests, its pending guests and the wardrobe.

Binding. Where and sizes. The page is the world’s Artifacts screen (68a) inside the production frame: the production rail at 206 episodic and 265 otherwise, then the hero — 56 top padding, the eyebrow at 11/.16em, the title at 52, the chip row 16 beneath — and a four-column grid at gap 20 in a 90 gutter, as the production’s Cast already draws it. Cards keep 68a’s bands: media frame 110, name 14/600 at 11 above the meta, meta 10.5 mono. The dashed cell spans two columns at min-height 176 and is the last cell of the grid, never its own band. There is no Generate door: a production reaches the bench through its own Generate, which answers to shots.

Binding · turn 100 Interactive video is a kind, the episode is a page with Arke on it, and a staged change is drawn where it will live (settles 99’s open question; retires 91b; supersedes 99b and 91c)

Binding. Interactive video is a kind of video, not a medium. A medium is what comes out — moving pictures, prose, sound — and interactive video is moving pictures. It has scenes, shots, takes and a cut like every other video; what it adds is a branch map and scenes that route by choice (turn 84, issue 401), which is exactly what a kind is for. Turn 84 put it on step one because step one was the only step; it has not belonged there since turn 83 split the two questions. Step one stays three — Video, Story, Audio — and step two becomes five.

Binding. The episode is a page with Arke on it, like the scene and the season. Episode Chat was the last level still drawn as somewhere to go: a conversation on one screen, what it produced on another, and an accept that moved you between them. Turn 97 settled this for the scene and turn 99 for the season, so the principle applies one level up unchanged. 91b is retired, the page keeps its promise, its scenes and Add scene, and the same docked panel carries the thread. One pattern at three scales, with nothing left over.

Binding. The screen shows what the conversation is making, while it makes it. A staged change is drawn where it will live — a proposed scene is a scene card in its place marked NEW · NOT WRITTEN YET, a changed promise line shows the new words marked STAGED — and the panel keeps only the count and the yes (2 scenes · 1 promise line). A field-by-field diff inside a chat asks a person to read a form to find out what just happened to their story; the story is the better display, and it is already on the screen. Turn 92 did this once by instinct with STAGED · NOT WRITTEN YET on a season tile; this makes it the rule at every level. This changes where a proposal is shown, never when it is written.

Binding. A staged thing is visible, not usable. The price of drawing proposals in place: until it is accepted it cannot be opened, counted as done, or dispatched. The counts say both and confuse neither — 5 scenes beside +2 staged, never 7 scenes — and the same holds for a scene the panel invented on the storyboard (turn 97’s suggested) and for money: nothing staged can reach the plan.

  • PR 1112 builds 145a: the row is a row again — the script typed on it, the title opening the page and the pencil editing, no Frame prompt toggle, no unfolding, a chevron beside the overflow, 14px above and below the frame — and the view row is Storyboard · Flow · Preview.

Binding · turn 145 A shot is a page — the list keeps the writing, the page holds the rest, and the Stage goes with the shot (supersedes 143, 139c and 14d; amends 138’s row, 135’s full-screen rule and 123’s four views)

Binding — a shot is a page. The scene lists its shots; a shot is opened, never unfolded. A press on a row’s number, frame or title, or on its chevron, opens …/scenes/:sceneId/shots/:shotId — the route 97’s Advanced used, whose sheet (14d) this page replaces. The row has no open state and no selected-and-closed state: a row is a row. Its ring is the list’s selection, which Flow and the dock follow (SPEC-036 R-25) and which opens nothing. 143’s four rules are withdrawn with the row that unfolded; 139c is withdrawn with the toggle.

Binding — the row keeps the writing. The script is typed on the row and saves on blur, 97’s founding rule kept; the title edits behind its pencil; nothing else on the list is an editor. The grip, the 285 × 208 frame with its number, duration and hover toolbar, and the 54 and 30 around it stay as 138 binds, with one amendment: 14px above and below the frame, so it sits inside the row rather than on its border (138’s bitmap and 139a set it flush; the row is 236 tall). On the list the frame identifies the shot, on the page it is judged. At the right: Regenerate or Generate frame, the overflow (Open in generator, Duplicate, Add shot after, Delete — Advanced and Stage this shot leave it, the page is both doors) and the chevron. Rows 18px apart, the place between them as 123 binds, the Grid as 139b binds with a press on a card opening the page.

Binding — the Shot view. Two columns. The frame whole at the production’s aspect, contained never cropped, filling the body’s height (292 × 519 at 9:16 in a 1360 × 850 frame; wider and shorter at 16:9, the frames tried for it beneath), with its number and duration chips and the same four-glyph toolbar the row has. Beside it the shot’s fields as cards with an icon and a name, in this order and no other: Script, Frame prompt, Notes, Camera, Timing, Continuity, Sound, Props. The column scrolls and the frame holds its place; nothing folds. Script is the row’s text, one record. Frame prompt is 139’s: the prompt the run sends, Authored once edited, View full prompt and Rebuild on its head, the references beneath as chips with what rides. Notes is one line until written in. Camera is 97’s nine — size, angle, lens, focus, movement, pace, lighting, time as selects with the label above, grade as a line — each reading from scene until set and carrying a dot once it overrides. Timing is duration, the row’s number, as a stepper, then the beats. Continuity is opens on the previous shot’s last frame, continues the previous shot (both inert on the first shot) and keep out of frame. Sound is dialogue, ambience, effects. Props is the states this shot cites. Aspect is the production’s and is not a control here; a per-shot aspect, if one is ever specified, is set where the shot’s record is edited and read on the timing line.

Binding — the Stage is the shot’s. The Stage leaves the scene’s view row, which is Storyboard · Flow · Preview from here. It is the second view of the shot page, as 140a and 144a draw it without the stepper line. Nothing under it changes: cast marks and sets stay the scene’s one record (scene.blocking), edited through whichever shot’s camera is open and said on the inspector’s blocking · shared line; the camera, its keys, the performances, the rig and the playblast stay the shot’s. Binding — the card follows the production’s aspect. A card’s frame is the production’s aspect, contained and never cropped (139): a 9:16 production stands its cards up, a 16:9 one lays them down. Binding · where a frame lands. A whole-scene run and a row’s Generate frame put the frame in its slot with the person still on the row. Neither leaves the scene, assembles the Cut, or gates a still on the Cut’s clock; that hand-off belongs to the Cut’s own controls.

Binding · turn 135 The scene’s cast is configured, not its header — a dashed box adds a character to the scene, a tile opens them, and what they carry rides into every shot that cites them: a word on the band, a node on the canvas, a clause in the plan (amends 123; retires the audio panels of PR 856)

Binding. The header is 123’s, plus one row. Breadcrumb, title, Review scene and Generate frames, the synopsis, the context chips and the count, and under them the cast: 32×32 tiles at radius 8, gap 6, 9 below the chips, in the order the characters first appear, closed by a dashed box of the same size carrying a plus. Nothing else. No warning, measurement, checkbox or disclosure computed for a dispatch sits on the page at rest. The whole-scene plan is not computed on render; it is computed when Plan video is pressed, for the plan card.

Binding. A character in a scene is the object. The scene’s cast is every character its shots cite by name (SPEC-029 R-23) plus every character added through the dashed box; a member with no citing shot says in no shot yet and stays until removed. Per member the scene stores at most two choices, voice and look, each an artifact by {id, hash}, versioned with the scene and written through one scene command so a name has one owner. Absent, they default to what the world already holds: the voice is the character’s designated sample (Voice page, 132) and the look is the kit’s portrait (SPEC-017). A read or image made for the scene is an artifact the scene holds, visible on the production’s artifacts page (134a) as linked: scene 4. The frame slot keeps its own rule (SPEC-036 §1.9); the playblast keeps its marker; the location takes this shape now, from its chip (below); the Cut’s music takes it later and is not drawn.

Binding. Four sizes, one object. In the header it is a tile. On the band it is the citation chip the build already draws, followed in mono by what rides in that shot: voice where the character speaks, look where they are seen, nothing where neither. On the canvas it is a node, 200×72, in the shot node’s card style, Open where the shot node carries Open in Storyboard, with dashed edges to the citing shots and voice · look · in N shots as its meta. In the plan it is a clause on the pass: Odile: voice, look. It is never a panel and never a heading.

Binding. The node is derived and the edge is soft. SPEC-029 R-24 as amended admits a node that is recomputed from the record on every render and authored by nothing; this node is a projection of the citations and the scene’s cast, stored nowhere itself. Its edges are not sequence edges: they never reorder, never pack, never carry a group. Dragging the node arranges the view (§1.16); Open on it opens the same dialog as the tile.

Binding. Adding is the dashed box, and it adds to the scene. The picker lists the production’s cast, then the world’s characters, as portrait cards with the name and the sheet version; a character already in the scene is listed, says in the scene, and does nothing when pressed. A press adds and closes. Nothing is asked at that moment, because voice and look have defaults. Remove from scene lives in the character dialog and nowhere else; it removes the member and the scene’s two choices, never an artifact and never a citation — a character a shot still cites comes straight back.

Binding. The character dialog. 820 wide, mounted on the app frame (SPEC-036 R-1). Left, 300, the full height of the card: the chosen look, and nothing else — it is a preview, not a control. Right: the name, then in mono the role, the sheet version and the derived speaks in / seen in; Look as a row of cards — the kit’s portrait, every image chosen for a scene, a dashed door that adds one — with the chosen one ringed; Voice as a row of cards in the same grammar; Lines in this scene as the script blocks she speaks, each with its read and a play dot, or no read yet; then Remove from scene and Done. A solid card is a choice and a press commits it; pressing a look changes the picture on the left. A dashed card is a door: Record a line and Generate a line produce a candidate to hear, and Keep files it as an artifact the scene holds and selects it, in one commit, with the provenance the audio foundation already records. Cost sits on the door that spends. A/B pins, speech-to-speech conversion, cadence controls and the performance bible are not drawn: they wait until the plain path is used, and when they return they belong to the character’s Voice page, not the scene.

Binding. The location is the first chip, and the chip opens the place. A scene has one location (SPEC-029 R-21’s inherited context), so it is not a member of the cast row and not a node on Flow — every shot has it, and an edge to each would say nothing; it is the canvas’s ground, said in the header on every view. The chip gains the plate at 16px, radius 5, and a press opens a dialog of the character’s shape: the plate large on the left, and on the right Plate as a row of cards — the kit’s establishing view, every view made for a scene, a dashed door that adds one — with the one in use ringed; pressing a card changes the picture. Change location opens the picker with the production’s locations first, then the world’s, and writes inherits.location through edit-scene, widened to carry inherits beside title and synopsis; today only Arke’s proposal path writes it. A scene with no location shows a dashed Add a location chip in the first slot, the same dashed door as the cast row’s box; a press opens the same picker, and choosing sets inherits.location and turns the chip into the place. Arke can set it too, through the proposal path it already uses. A scene never needs a place to hold shots; without one, no plate rides. A shot that overrides the location keeps its own chip on its band, as today. The plate rides as a look on every shot set there, so the plan card says The counting room: plate on every pass, and the Generate frames dialog lists it in its References rows like a cited sheet. Time and look stay words on chips. Ambience is not drawn.

Binding. What will be sent is said where the money moves, and only there. Dispatch resolves each cited character’s scene voice and look into that shot’s references at plan time, so nothing is chosen per dispatch. The Generate frames dialog’s References list shows the looks beside the cited sheets in the rows it already has — rides, or one clause on the thing refused: this model takes one image. The plan card says per pass what rides, per character. The Bench’s reference review does the same for a shot or board rendered to video, with riding / not riding as it already does for sheets, and a route that carries no audio says takes no audio once, on the voice. Timing is one clause on the pass it changes — not on the Cut · uses its 5.0s — and appears nowhere else. Never on the header, never as a shot id.

Binding. Flow and Stage go full screen from one glyph. The right end of the view row carries a 26×26 glyph button (lucide maximize-2 at 14px, the pin’s weight) on Flow and Stage, and on no other view: Storyboard is a column that gains nothing from width, and Preview may take it with the turn that draws it. A press fills the app frame with the view alone — the production rail, the header, the view row and the dock leave together — and leaves three things: a pill at top-left naming the production, episode, scene and view; the same glyph reversed at top-right with Esc, either of which returns; and the view’s own controls where they already sit, Flow’s zoom cluster and Stage’s panel and timeline. It is session state like the put-away (R-28), never a setting, and it changes no record: selection, zoom and node positions carry across both ways (R-25, §1.16), and the dock’s thread waits untouched. Stage full screen is the viewport with its panel and timeline, named and not drawn, as turn 123 left the Stage.

Binding. What leaves the scene page. Table read becomes Play lines on Preview, playing the cast’s reads in shot order; not drawn, because Preview is not. Rehearsal notes leave the scene. Dialogue guidance is not drawn and returns, if its catalogue ever holds an entry, as a refusal clause in the References list. Visual facts are not drawn. The prose sections turn-120 to turn-126 are removed from both master files; a limit in them that is still true is a rule here or a line in the private spec set, never a screen.

PR 1112 moves it onto the shot page as its second view (145d): the filmstrip steps, the stepper line goes, and the staging’s words sit on the view row beside the full-screen glyph; every door to it — a Flow staging node, a blockout or playblast Arke was asked for — opens that shot’s page on it.

Binding · turn 145 A shot is a page — the list keeps the writing, the page holds the rest, and the Stage goes with the shot (supersedes 143, 139c and 14d; amends 138’s row, 135’s full-screen rule and 123’s four views)

Binding — a shot is a page. The scene lists its shots; a shot is opened, never unfolded. A press on a row’s number, frame or title, or on its chevron, opens …/scenes/:sceneId/shots/:shotId — the route 97’s Advanced used, whose sheet (14d) this page replaces. The row has no open state and no selected-and-closed state: a row is a row. Its ring is the list’s selection, which Flow and the dock follow (SPEC-036 R-25) and which opens nothing. 143’s four rules are withdrawn with the row that unfolded; 139c is withdrawn with the toggle.

Binding — the row keeps the writing. The script is typed on the row and saves on blur, 97’s founding rule kept; the title edits behind its pencil; nothing else on the list is an editor. The grip, the 285 × 208 frame with its number, duration and hover toolbar, and the 54 and 30 around it stay as 138 binds, with one amendment: 14px above and below the frame, so it sits inside the row rather than on its border (138’s bitmap and 139a set it flush; the row is 236 tall). On the list the frame identifies the shot, on the page it is judged. At the right: Regenerate or Generate frame, the overflow (Open in generator, Duplicate, Add shot after, Delete — Advanced and Stage this shot leave it, the page is both doors) and the chevron. Rows 18px apart, the place between them as 123 binds, the Grid as 139b binds with a press on a card opening the page.

Binding — the head of the page. The breadcrumb ends on the scene and is the way back; the footer’s link says Back to scene. The title is Shot 1 · Odile counts the hours at --type-title with the pencil; at its right one primary — Generate frame on a shot without one, Regenerate with one — and the overflow (Open in generator, Play from here, Duplicate, Delete). Under the title the filmstrip: every shot of the scene at 40 × 71 (the production’s aspect, cropped, the number on each), the open one ringed, ‹ and › at its ends and on the keyboard’s arrows, and Shot 1 of 4 at the right; a press opens that shot in the same view. It is the row’s chevron seen from the other side and the Stage’s stepper, which is why 144a’s ‹ Shot 1 › line goes. Then the view row, Shot · Stage, with the state word at its right: on Shot the frame’s (Frame ready, Needs frame, generating, stale, failed), on Stage the staging’s (v3 · 3 keys · push in) beside the full-screen glyph.

Binding — the Shot view. Two columns. The frame whole at the production’s aspect, contained never cropped, filling the body’s height (292 × 519 at 9:16 in a 1360 × 850 frame; wider and shorter at 16:9, the frames tried for it beneath), with its number and duration chips and the same four-glyph toolbar the row has. Beside it the shot’s fields as cards with an icon and a name, in this order and no other: Script, Frame prompt, Notes, Camera, Timing, Continuity, Sound, Props. The column scrolls and the frame holds its place; nothing folds. Script is the row’s text, one record. Frame prompt is 139’s: the prompt the run sends, Authored once edited, View full prompt and Rebuild on its head, the references beneath as chips with what rides. Notes is one line until written in. Camera is 97’s nine — size, angle, lens, focus, movement, pace, lighting, time as selects with the label above, grade as a line — each reading from scene until set and carrying a dot once it overrides. Timing is duration, the row’s number, as a stepper, then the beats. Continuity is opens on the previous shot’s last frame, continues the previous shot (both inert on the first shot) and keep out of frame. Sound is dialogue, ambience, effects. Props is the states this shot cites. Aspect is the production’s and is not a control here; a per-shot aspect, if one is ever specified, is set where the shot’s record is edited and read on the timing line.

Binding — the Stage is the shot’s. The Stage leaves the scene’s view row, which is Storyboard · Flow · Preview from here. It is the second view of the shot page, as 140a and 144a draw it without the stepper line. Nothing under it changes: cast marks and sets stay the scene’s one record (scene.blocking), edited through whichever shot’s camera is open and said on the inspector’s blocking · shared line; the camera, its keys, the performances, the rig and the playblast stay the shot’s. Build with Arke already takes a shot. Full screen from the glyph as 135 binds, the way out on the head row as 144 binds; 135’s glyph on the scene’s view row is now Flow’s alone. Preview stays the scene’s: it plays the scene, and Play from here in the page’s overflow is its door.

Binding — the Grid is the default. The storyboard opens on the Grid, and Grid stands first in the control: Grid · List. 138’s List is the default authoring layout is withdrawn with the authoring that left the row; the List is where the script is read and written at width and where the boards show, and showing boards shows the List, as the build already does. The choice is remembered per person, not per scene, and is never written to the world.

Binding — the card follows the production’s aspect. A card’s frame is the production’s aspect, contained and never cropped (139): a 9:16 production stands its cards up, a 16:9 one lays them down. There is no scene aspect — a route takes one aspect per request and a cut cannot hold two (97) — so every card in a scene is one shape, and a per-shot aspect, if one is ever specified, shows on that card alone. Columns follow it: four across at portrait, three at landscape at 1360, one fewer whenever a card would fall under 176 wide at portrait or 280 at landscape, so a landscape frame on a card is as wide as the List’s and a portrait one never smaller than the filmstrip’s.

Binding — the Grid card. 139b stands — the same shots, order and selection, the frame whole at the production’s aspect, title, timing, the script clamped to three lines at rest and growing while typed — less the Frame prompt toggle, and with the chevron on its foot beside the overflow. A press on the frame, the title or the chevron opens the page; the grip drags, and the place between two cards is where a shot goes, as between two rows.

Binding — the dock follows. On the page the dock is Arke · Shot 1, the shot’s title and the scene’s version beneath, the composer saying this shot; the thread is the shot’s, and a result card names what it changed. No model select, as 143 binds for the scene. Flow, Stage and the Bench are unchanged in what they hold; the production’s and the episode’s docks keep their select.

Binding · turn 144 The Stage panel is an inspector — what is on the stage, then one form for the selection, in one field grammar with a fixed label column; and the way out of full screen sits on the head row (amends 140’s panel and its full-screen rule)

Binding · the inspector. The panel holds the stage list and one form. The list is what is on the stage — the camera, every figure, every set, one line each with a mark, its name and its state in mono — and pressing a line is the same selection the viewport makes: one selection, held once. The form beneath is the selected thing’s and nothing else’s: the camera’s key, a figure, a set, or, with nothing selected, the shot. The list ends in Add set; figures come from the scene’s cast. The playblast’s state and the two ways on (Export playblast, Render with this) are the shot’s whatever is selected, so they sit pinned under every form rather than in the shot’s alone.

Binding · one field grammar. A row is 24px: a label in a 64px column, lowercase in mono at --text-2xs, then the control, which starts at the label column’s edge on every row of every form. A number is its value with its unit and the stepper at the right end (1.60 m, 0 °, 35 mm, 0.25); a choice is a 24px select; an either/or is chips; a yes/no is a 12px box; three of a kind (x y z, w h d, pitch turn roll) share one row under one label; a name is a 24px field; a way on is an underlined word. No browser input, no sentence-case label, no full-width stack. A section is an eyebrow with its meta at the right end and a rule above it; there is no other heading.

Binding · the way out of full screen. The exit is the glyph reversed at the right end of the shot’s head row, after the version and key count, a 32px bordered button on --secondary — the row a person is already reading, where the way in stood. The pill at the top left names the place and is not a control. Esc leaves as before. The corner pill of 140b goes.

Binding · the panel’s width. 264px, in the workspace and in full screen; the viewport gives up the 26px. The list and a form fit the panel without scrolling in full screen; in the workspace the panel scrolls as one column.

Binding · turn 142 The Bench’s keyframe slots, the voice-references control and Presets — drawn after they shipped, so the dispatch row has a drawing to be held to (amends 68b and 68c)

Binding · the Keyframe lane. The lane exists only where the model verifies a frame mode. Its tiles are the pictures the shot must pass through, in order: the first carries start, the second end, and the add tile names the slot it fills — Start frame, then End frame, then Add frame where a model takes more. At the lane’s ceiling the add tile leaves; it is never disabled. A picture on the lane is Image 1, Image 2, and the brief cites it by that name, so a rewrite that drops the citation is refused rather than sent. What the route does with the pictures is the Keyframe control’s hint (Seedance 2.0 Fast · image-to-video · takes a start frame and an end frame · the Stage playblast does not ride), not a caption above the composer: the two-line camera notice and the line under the prompt go, per 137.

Binding · voice references are an option chip. voice refs · on sits in the option row beside duration, aspect and resolution, and toggles like them. Off, it reads voice refs · off. What rides is said where it lands: the take’s own chip (voice refs rode) and the receipt, not a paragraph under the checkbox. A route that takes no audio says so once, on the chip’s hint (this model takes no audio), and the chip is absent when no cast in the shot has a voice.

Binding · one dispatch row. Nothing wraps into the row; a long label belongs on a chip or a hint. The running route is named on the session line and the take (image-to-video), never only its family name.

builtwhat shipped
  • The library beside the cut with one drag engine and posters by artifact id (PR 1054); typed trims in the Inspector and audio import (PR 944); the export sheet at /cut?export=1 owns delivery.
Binding · turn 122 The Inspector stops sharing the edge with Arke and sits above it — a tool and a collaborator are not alternatives, and three things that were never the selection leave the panel (amends 121’s tabbed pane; completes turn 120 by removing its one exception)

Binding. The right edge is Arke’s, and the Inspector is its guest. Turn 121 drew them as two tabs, which asserts they are alternatives. They are not the same kind of thing: the Inspector is a tool, scoped to the selection, changed by every click, and it authors; Arke is a collaborator, scoped to the whole cut and unchanged as the selection moves. Tabbing them means consulting one costs the other at exactly the moment both are wanted — I have shot 13 selected and I want to say hold it longer. They stack: the Inspector above, Arke below, one edge.

Binding. The Inspector exists only when something is selected. Nothing selected and the edge is Arke at full height (122a), identical to the season, the episode and a scene — which is what makes turn 120’s rule true without an exception for this screen. There is no nothing selected panel because, once the three things below are removed, it has nothing left to say.

Binding. Three things leave the Inspector, because none of them is the selection. The cut’s own summary — duration, clips, lanes, coverage — is already the header two inches away (0:39 · 4 of 5 shots covered). Needs a decision was the gap’s third statement, after the lane draws it at its own length and the footer counts it. Export preset belongs behind Export film, where a person goes to change it; it was in the pane because the pane had room, which is the worst reason for anything to be anywhere.

Binding. What that costs is said: the standing list of decisions goes. There is no longer a panel that lists every unresolved thing in the cut. That is a real loss and a small one at this size — the gap is drawn in the lane where it happens, counted in the footer, and selectable, and selecting it gives the Inspector that fixes it (122c): Fill from shot 13, Cut it short, Open in Generate, with Arke beneath already talking about the same shot. A decision is made where it is drawn. If a cut ever carries enough of them to need a list, the list belongs in the footer that already counts them, not in a panel that has to be opened to be believed.

Binding. Arke keeps a floor and the Inspector keeps a ceiling. The Inspector is capped at half the edge and scrolls inside it, so a selection with a lot to author — a subtitle cue with its sources and a transcribe control, a sound clip with its gain — cannot squeeze the composer off the screen. It can also be collapsed to its title. The composer is the one control that must never need scrolling to reach, because it is how everything else on this screen gets asked for.

Binding. Arke’s panel is 330px everywhere, the Cut included. It was 306 here only because it was sharing a pane sized for a property sheet. One width, one position, one closed state (turn 120’s strip): the assistant is the same object on every page of a production, and a person should never have to look for it twice.

builtwhat shipped
  • Turn 147 records the shipped episode/scene/shot scope, selectable playable cards and shared verdict bar for the picked take. The bar acts on the selected card; it is not duplicated on each card (issue 1165).
  • Measured durations use one decimal. Accepted contact-sheet frames name their shot and mark acceptance as done.
Binding · turn 147 The takes in context — the built episode, scene and shot filters, and the selected take's verdict (issue 1165; updates 102c)

Labels describe the work. Measured take durations round to one decimal; whole seconds have no trailing zero. Contact-sheet frames use their shot title, with the file name available as a tooltip; an accepted frame reads Accepted and cannot be accepted again. In the Cut, Take N and its model identify the candidate, while its immutable id stays in the tooltip. Episode rail labels use sorted position, retaining the duplicate-order warning without changing the saved record. A preview image exists only while its frame-clock source is a still.

builtwhat shipped
  • The canvas over layoutRouting (branch-map.tsx, lib/branch-map.ts): cards with the scene’s first shot frame, curves with labels, dashed until walked, the tray, the legend, zoom and fit; wheel pans, Ctrl or Cmd with the wheel zooms, a drag on the ground pans.
  • The header counts every blocking finding, the export’s own number, and the warnings bar unvisited routes. No minimap yet past 60 scenes.
Binding · turn 157 The branch map is drawn — a canvas of the routing file, findings drawn where they are and counted in the header, every edit a gesture on the map with the Inspector as its second way in (draws the map turn 84 bound; applies the Interactive-video brief rev 1 §3–§4; follows 122’s edge and 100’s staging; replaces turn 156’s built-not-drawn note)

Binding. The map is a canvas, laid out by the file and never by hand. Layers run left to right by longest path from the start, in-layer order by the first authored choice into each scene, then id — layoutRouting as built — so the same graph always draws the same picture and nobody can drag a card somewhere it will not stay. Cards are 148 wide: the scene’s frame at 16:9, its title, and one meta line (its length and ways out; an ending’s title behind a flag). Layers sit 120 apart so a label fits between them. A choice is a curve from the right edge of one card to the left of the next with an arrowhead; one that skips a layer arcs over it, never through a card; a scene two routes reach is one card with two arrows in, never a copy. The canvas is the dotted ground on --background, and opens fitted to the window.

Binding. Designations are marks on the card, in words. The start is ringed (2px --foreground, 3 out) and tagged Start; an ending is tagged Ending with its title on the meta line; a scene reached two ways carries the warning glyph beside its meta. Scenes on no route sit in a tray under the map, Not on a route, dashed: an excluded scene dimmed to 55% with its reason in italics, an unreachable one outlined in --destructive and tagged Unreachable. Colour is only ever a finding’s: the map is otherwise the neutral chrome, so the scenes’ frames carry it.

Binding. Walk evidence is drawn on the edge. A choice walked in preview at its current ends is a solid line and a solid label; one nobody has walked is dashed, line and label, and the legend at the foot says which is which. That is the whole of the untraversed-edge finding, drawn where it lives, and it clears itself on the map the moment the preview walks it.

Binding. Findings are counted in the header and listed only when asked. Turn 122 put a decision where it is drawn and the count where it is seen, and turn 84 wants a list with every finding by name; both hold. The header carries 4 block and 2 warn beside Preview and the export, whose label is the blocking count (Export blocked · 4) until it reads Export web package. The count is a selection: pressed, the Inspector above Arke (157b) lists them, blocks first, each named by scene or choice, with its evidence and the press that clears it — Draw a choice to it and Exclude… for a scene with no way in, Preview a route that walks them for choices nobody has walked, which folds the unvisited-route warning into the finding it restates. Selecting a finding outlines what it names on the map. No score, no percentage, no health.

Binding. Every edit is a gesture on the map, with the Inspector as its second way in. Drag from a card’s out-port (it shows on hover and on the selected card) and drop on another card to draw a choice; the label field opens on the new edge, and Enter commits it through the gate as one routing.json change (157c). A selected choice thickens, inverts its label, and its arrowhead becomes the handle that retargets it (157d); a selected scene offers the start, an ending with its title and an exclusion with its reason (157f). Every one of those is also a field or a press in the Inspector, so none needs a pointer. Every save moves the routing version, whichever way it came in — the number in the header is the one the preview’s evidence and the package’s saved place key on.

Binding. A removal names what it breaks before it happens. Remove choice (or Delete on a focused edge) opens a confirmation whose body is the consequence, computed from the file as it would be: a scene left with no way in, a choice left hanging from a scene no route reaches, an ending no longer reachable (157e). The things named are outlined on the map while it is open. A removal that breaks nothing says so and still asks once.

Binding. Arke stages on the map. Turn 100’s rule at the map’s scale: a proposed choice is drawn where it will live, dotted, with Staged on its label; a proposed start, ending or exclusion is a Staged tag on the card it touches. The panel keeps the count (1 choice · 1 exclusion) and Accept. Nothing staged is counted in the header’s findings, offered in the preview, or retargetable (157h).

Binding. Day one is one card. An interactive production with scenes and no routing opens on Draw the first choice from the start scene, the scenes as their frames to pick from and Start at <scene> as the press (157g) — the built press, now with a choice of scene. It writes a start and nothing else; the map draws with every other scene in the tray and the start’s out-port showing. No scenes yet keeps the built empty state and its one line.

Binding. The map is one tab stop, and walks as it draws. A listbox, as built: Tab reaches it, the arrows walk cards and then their choices in layout order, Home and End jump to the start and the last, Enter selects into the Inspector, Delete removes with the confirmation above, P previews from the focused scene. +, − and 0 zoom and fit, as the control at the foot does; past 60 scenes the foot gains a minimap. A scene is announced as its title, its ways in and out; a choice as its label, from and to, and whether it has been walked.

Binding. Below 900 wide, the same map as a list. Layers top to bottom, each scene a row with its frame, each choice a goes to row under it with its label, dashed where not walked (157i). The same order as the canvas, the same selection and the same Inspector; no sideways scroll of the page.

Binding · turn 157 The branch map is drawn — a canvas of the routing file, findings drawn where they are and counted in the header, every edit a gesture on the map with the Inspector as its second way in (draws the map turn 84 bound; applies the Interactive-video brief rev 1 §3–§4; follows 122’s edge and 100’s staging; replaces turn 156’s built-not-drawn note)

Binding. The map is a canvas, laid out by the file and never by hand. Layers run left to right by longest path from the start, in-layer order by the first authored choice into each scene, then id — layoutRouting as built — so the same graph always draws the same picture and nobody can drag a card somewhere it will not stay. Cards are 148 wide: the scene’s frame at 16:9, its title, and one meta line (its length and ways out; an ending’s title behind a flag). Layers sit 120 apart so a label fits between them. A choice is a curve from the right edge of one card to the left of the next with an arrowhead; one that skips a layer arcs over it, never through a card; a scene two routes reach is one card with two arrows in, never a copy. The canvas is the dotted ground on --background, and opens fitted to the window.

Binding. Designations are marks on the card, in words. The start is ringed (2px --foreground, 3 out) and tagged Start; an ending is tagged Ending with its title on the meta line; a scene reached two ways carries the warning glyph beside its meta. Scenes on no route sit in a tray under the map, Not on a route, dashed: an excluded scene dimmed to 55% with its reason in italics, an unreachable one outlined in --destructive and tagged Unreachable. Colour is only ever a finding’s: the map is otherwise the neutral chrome, so the scenes’ frames carry it.

Binding. Walk evidence is drawn on the edge. A choice walked in preview at its current ends is a solid line and a solid label; one nobody has walked is dashed, line and label, and the legend at the foot says which is which. That is the whole of the untraversed-edge finding, drawn where it lives, and it clears itself on the map the moment the preview walks it.

Binding. Findings are counted in the header and listed only when asked. Turn 122 put a decision where it is drawn and the count where it is seen, and turn 84 wants a list with every finding by name; both hold. The header carries 4 block and 2 warn beside Preview and the export, whose label is the blocking count (Export blocked · 4) until it reads Export web package. The count is a selection: pressed, the Inspector above Arke (157b) lists them, blocks first, each named by scene or choice, with its evidence and the press that clears it — Draw a choice to it and Exclude… for a scene with no way in, Preview a route that walks them for choices nobody has walked, which folds the unvisited-route warning into the finding it restates. Selecting a finding outlines what it names on the map. No score, no percentage, no health.

Binding. Every edit is a gesture on the map, with the Inspector as its second way in. Drag from a card’s out-port (it shows on hover and on the selected card) and drop on another card to draw a choice; the label field opens on the new edge, and Enter commits it through the gate as one routing.json change (157c). A selected choice thickens, inverts its label, and its arrowhead becomes the handle that retargets it (157d); a selected scene offers the start, an ending with its title and an exclusion with its reason (157f). Every one of those is also a field or a press in the Inspector, so none needs a pointer. Every save moves the routing version, whichever way it came in — the number in the header is the one the preview’s evidence and the package’s saved place key on.

Binding. A removal names what it breaks before it happens. Remove choice (or Delete on a focused edge) opens a confirmation whose body is the consequence, computed from the file as it would be: a scene left with no way in, a choice left hanging from a scene no route reaches, an ending no longer reachable (157e). The things named are outlined on the map while it is open. A removal that breaks nothing says so and still asks once.

Binding. Arke stages on the map. Turn 100’s rule at the map’s scale: a proposed choice is drawn where it will live, dotted, with Staged on its label; a proposed start, ending or exclusion is a Staged tag on the card it touches. The panel keeps the count (1 choice · 1 exclusion) and Accept. Nothing staged is counted in the header’s findings, offered in the preview, or retargetable (157h).

Binding. Day one is one card. An interactive production with scenes and no routing opens on Draw the first choice from the start scene, the scenes as their frames to pick from and Start at <scene> as the press (157g) — the built press, now with a choice of scene. It writes a start and nothing else; the map draws with every other scene in the tray and the start’s out-port showing. No scenes yet keeps the built empty state and its one line.

Binding. The map is one tab stop, and walks as it draws. A listbox, as built: Tab reaches it, the arrows walk cards and then their choices in layout order, Home and End jump to the start and the last, Enter selects into the Inspector, Delete removes with the confirmation above, P previews from the focused scene. +, − and 0 zoom and fit, as the control at the foot does; past 60 scenes the foot gains a minimap. A scene is announced as its title, its ways in and out; a choice as its label, from and to, and whether it has been walked.

Binding. Below 900 wide, the same map as a list. Layers top to bottom, each scene a row with its frame, each choice a goes to row under it with its label, dashed where not walked (157i). The same order as the canvas, the same selection and the same Inspector; no sideways scroll of the page.

Colour is only ever a finding’s: the map is otherwise the neutral chrome, so the scenes’ frames carry it.

Binding. Walk evidence is drawn on the edge. A choice walked in preview at its current ends is a solid line and a solid label; one nobody has walked is dashed, line and label, and the legend at the foot says which is which. That is the whole of the untraversed-edge finding, drawn where it lives, and it clears itself on the map the moment the preview walks it.

Binding. Findings are counted in the header and listed only when asked. Turn 122 put a decision where it is drawn and the count where it is seen, and turn 84 wants a list with every finding by name; both hold. The header carries 4 block and 2 warn beside Preview and the export, whose label is the blocking count (Export blocked · 4) until it reads Export web package. The count is a selection: pressed, the Inspector above Arke (157b) lists them, blocks first, each named by scene or choice, with its evidence and the press that clears it — Draw a choice to it and Exclude… for a scene with no way in, Preview a route that walks them for choices nobody has walked, which folds the unvisited-route warning into the finding it restates. Selecting a finding outlines what it names on the map. No score, no percentage, no health.

Binding. Every edit is a gesture on the map, with the Inspector as its second way in. Drag from a card’s out-port (it shows on hover and on the selected card) and drop on another card to draw a choice; the label field opens on the new edge, and Enter commits it through the gate as one routing.json change (157c). A selected choice thickens, inverts its label, and its arrowhead becomes the handle that retargets it (157d); a selected scene offers the start, an ending with its title and an exclusion with its reason (157f). Every one of those is also a field or a press in the Inspector, so none needs a pointer. Every save moves the routing version, whichever way it came in — the number in the header is the one the preview’s evidence and the package’s saved place key on.

Binding. A removal names what it breaks before it happens. Remove choice (or Delete on a focused edge) opens a confirmation whose body is the consequence, computed from the file as it would be: a scene left with no way in, a choice left hanging from a scene no route reaches, an ending no longer reachable (157e). The things named are outlined on the map while it is open. A removal that breaks nothing says so and still asks once.

Binding. Arke stages on the map. Turn 100’s rule at the map’s scale: a proposed choice is drawn where it will live, dotted, with Staged on its label; a proposed start, ending or exclusion is a Staged tag on the card it touches. The panel keeps the count (1 choice · 1 exclusion) and Accept. Nothing staged is counted in the header’s findings, offered in the preview, or retargetable (157h).

Binding. Day one is one card. An interactive production with scenes and no routing opens on Draw the first choice from the start scene, the scenes as their frames to pick from and Start at <scene> as the press (157g) — the built press, now with a choice of scene. It writes a start and nothing else; the map draws with every other scene in the tray and the start’s out-port showing. No scenes yet keeps the built empty state and its one line.

Binding. The map is one tab stop, and walks as it draws. A listbox, as built: Tab reaches it, the arrows walk cards and then their choices in layout order, Home and End jump to the start and the last, Enter selects into the Inspector, Delete removes with the confirmation above, P previews from the focused scene. +, − and 0 zoom and fit, as the control at the foot does; past 60 scenes the foot gains a minimap. A scene is announced as its title, its ways in and out; a choice as its label, from and to, and whether it has been walked.

Binding. Below 900 wide, the same map as a list. Layers top to bottom, each scene a row with its frame, each choice a goes to row under it with its label, dashed where not walked (157i). The same order as the canvas, the same selection and the same Inspector; no sideways scroll of the page.

Binding. The map is a canvas, laid out by the file and never by hand. Layers run left to right by longest path from the start, in-layer order by the first authored choice into each scene, then id — layoutRouting as built — so the same graph always draws the same picture and nobody can drag a card somewhere it will not stay. A choice is a curve from the right edge of one card to the left of the next with an arrowhead; one that skips a layer arcs over it, never through a card; a scene two routes reach is one card with two arrows in, never a copy. The canvas is the dotted ground on --background, and opens fitted to the window.

builtwhat shipped
  • The package's own player over the whole window (components/interactive-player.tsx mounting contracts/src/interactive-player.js), with the author's strip: where it started, how many choices nobody has walked, Branch map, Close preview and Esc.
  • A scene plays its accepted clips in shot order, a pass covering several shots once; a pressed choice records walk evidence, and its not walked mark and the strip's count fall as the findings come back.
Binding · turn 156 Interactive video gets its player — one player for the preview and the package, the picture full-bleed, the choice rising out of the scene’s last frame (draws the player turn 84 deferred; applies the Interactive-video brief rev 1 §5–§6; amends nothing drawn)

Binding. One player, two homes. The preview in the app and the exported player.html are the same player: the same layout, the same controls, the same keys and the same playback state. The app adds one thing, the author’s strip (156g); the package adds nothing. What a person previews is what a viewer gets, which is only true if one piece of code draws both — a framework-free module the client mounts and the exporter inlines, never two players kept alike by hand.

Binding. The picture is the page. The player fills its window on --media-overlay-bg whatever the app’s theme, letterboxing a picture whose aspect differs and never cropping it (a 9:16 production on a phone fills it, 156i). The chrome is type and icons over two scrims — 168 at the top, 300 at the foot — in --media-overlay-fg, with no panels behind the transport. It shows on a pointer move, a touch or any key, and rests after 2.5s of stillness while playing; it never rests while paused, and a choice on screen keeps only the title. The top holds the production as an eyebrow and the scene’s title in h3; the scene title is the only place the player names where you are.

Binding. The transport is the scene’s. The scrubber runs across this scene only, because a route has no length until it ends and a film-long bar would be a guess; a fork glyph at its right end marks where the choice waits. Under it: play or pause, back 10 seconds, volume and the time as 0:48 / 1:12 on the left; captions, the route and full screen on the right, each a 40 round icon button with its name. Keys: Space or K play and pause, ← and → five seconds, M mute, C captions, R the route, F full screen, 1–4 a choice. Captions are the scene cut’s WebVTT, drawn centred above the transport and lifted above the cards while a choice is up.

Binding. The choice rises out of the last frame. When the scene ends its last frame holds under a 34% dim and the foot scrim, and the choices rise into the lower third in authored order: cards 344 by 72, 16 apart, radius 16, glass (--media-overlay-bg at 46% over a 22px blur, a 22% hairline), the label in h3 and its key number in a 26 square before it. The first card holds focus, and focus inverts a card to --media-overlay-fg ground — monochrome, as the chrome is, so the picture carries the colour. Replay scene sits under the cards. There is no question over them: the routing file holds a label per choice and nothing else, and a prompt the author cannot write is not the player’s to invent. A press holds the chosen card for 300ms, the others fall away, and the next scene cuts in. A scene with one choice still waits for it; the label is the author’s word for going on.

Binding. Untimed is the default, and the only built behaviour. A timed choice (156c) is held: a per-production option, off unless set, that needs a default the author names — a line drains under the cards, the default card says default, and Space pauses the choice. It is a presentation setting of the production, never a field of routing.json, which stays the graph and nothing else. Until it is built nothing in either player counts down.

Binding. The viewer’s place is all the player keeps. The route (156d) is the playback state drawn: the scenes watched, a 96 by 54 still of each, and the choice taken between them, in a glass sheet 420 wide over the picture, which keeps playing. Choose again on a past choice goes back to that choice point and drops the route after it; Start over goes to the start. Nothing else is drawn because nothing else exists: no endings found, no percentage seen, no locked or unseen hints — statistics are among what this medium cannot hold (turn 78), and the state { sceneId, positionSec, route, updatedAt } has nowhere to keep them.

Binding. An ending is a title, not a result. The last frame holds under a left scrim, ENDING as the eyebrow, the ending’s title at text-5xl — the largest type the player sets — and the route beneath as stills joined by the choice labels, the ending’s own still ringed. Start again is the primary; Back to last choice the second. A scene with no choices that is not an ending cannot be published, so a viewer never meets an ending without a title.

Binding. A return visit opens on where you were. A saved place opens the package on its poster (156f): the world as eyebrow, the production’s title, Continue with the scene and time under a thin bar, and Start over. The place is saved on this device only and per routing version, as the package already keys it; a package exported from a newer routing opens fresh, because an old route may name a choice that is gone. Without a saved place the poster is the start scene’s first frame and the one button reads Play.

Binding. The preview is the player plus one strip. From the branch map’s Preview from here the player takes the whole window (156g), and Esc returns to the map where it was. The strip, 56 tall, says Preview, where it started, how many choices nobody has walked, Branch map and Close preview. A card whose choice has no walk evidence carries not walked; pressing it walks it, and the count falls. A scene plays its whole cut — its accepted takes in shot order — not its first shot. A scene with no accepted take plays as a slate (156h) and its choices still walk, as built.

The player fills its window on --media-overlay-bg whatever the app’s theme, letterboxing a picture whose aspect differs and never cropping it (a 9:16 production on a phone fills it, 156i). The chrome is type and icons over two scrims — 168 at the top, 300 at the foot — in --media-overlay-fg, with no panels behind the transport. It shows on a pointer move, a touch or any key, and rests after 2.5s of stillness while playing; it never rests while paused, and a choice on screen keeps only the title. The top holds the production as an eyebrow and the scene’s title in h3; the scene title is the only place the player names where you are.

Binding. The transport is the scene’s. The scrubber runs across this scene only, because a route has no length until it ends and a film-long bar would be a guess; a fork glyph at its right end marks where the choice waits. Under it: play or pause, back 10 seconds, volume and the time as 0:48 / 1:12 on the left; captions, the route and full screen on the right, each a 40 round icon button with its name. Keys: Space or K play and pause, ← and → five seconds, M mute, C captions, R the route, F full screen, 1–4 a choice. Captions are the scene cut’s WebVTT, drawn centred above the transport and lifted above the cards while a choice is up.

Binding. The choice rises out of the last frame. When the scene ends its last frame holds under a 34% dim and the foot scrim, and the choices rise into the lower third in authored order: cards 344 by 72, 16 apart, radius 16, glass (--media-overlay-bg at 46% over a 22px blur, a 22% hairline), the label in h3 and its key number in a 26 square before it. The first card holds focus, and focus inverts a card to --media-overlay-fg ground — monochrome, as the chrome is, so the picture carries the colour. Replay scene sits under the cards. There is no question over them: the routing file holds a label per choice and nothing else, and a prompt the author cannot write is not the player’s to invent. A press holds the chosen card for 300ms, the others fall away, and the next scene cuts in. A scene with one choice still waits for it; the label is the author’s word for going on.

Binding. Untimed is the default, and the only built behaviour. A timed choice (156c) is held: a per-production option, off unless set, that needs a default the author names — a line drains under the cards, the default card says default, and Space pauses the choice. It is a presentation setting of the production, never a field of routing.json, which stays the graph and nothing else. Until it is built nothing in either player counts down.

Binding. The viewer’s place is all the player keeps. The route (156d) is the playback state drawn: the scenes watched, a 96 by 54 still of each, and the choice taken between them, in a glass sheet 420 wide over the picture, which keeps playing. Choose again on a past choice goes back to that choice point and drops the route after it; Start over goes to the start. Nothing else is drawn because nothing else exists: no endings found, no percentage seen, no locked or unseen hints — statistics are among what this medium cannot hold (turn 78), and the state { sceneId, positionSec, route, updatedAt } has nowhere to keep them.

Binding. An ending is a title, not a result. The last frame holds under a left scrim, ENDING as the eyebrow, the ending’s title at text-5xl — the largest type the player sets — and the route beneath as stills joined by the choice labels, the ending’s own still ringed. Start again is the primary; Back to last choice the second. A scene with no choices that is not an ending cannot be published, so a viewer never meets an ending without a title.

Binding. A return visit opens on where you were. A saved place opens the package on its poster (156f): the world as eyebrow, the production’s title, Continue with the scene and time under a thin bar, and Start over. The place is saved on this device only and per routing version, as the package already keys it; a package exported from a newer routing opens fresh, because an old route may name a choice that is gone. Without a saved place the poster is the start scene’s first frame and the one button reads Play.

Binding. The preview is the player plus one strip. From the branch map’s Preview from here the player takes the whole window (156g), and Esc returns to the map where it was. The strip, 56 tall, says Preview, where it started, how many choices nobody has walked, Branch map and Close preview. A card whose choice has no walk evidence carries not walked; pressing it walks it, and the count falls. A scene plays its whole cut — its accepted takes in shot order — not its first shot. A scene with no accepted take plays as a slate (156h) and its choices still walk, as built.

New production · what kind of interactive

built · drifted#/w/:worldId/productions/new · CHOOSEchecked 2026-09-27
174a in the master →

Step two of CHOOSE asks one question now. The CHOOSE card leads to a step that until now asked only for a name. It now asks what kind of interactive: Interactive movie (the branching film we have today) or Visual novel (pictures, text and voices, read at the viewer’s own pace). Each is named for what the viewer does, watch or read, and the line under it says so. The door keeps three cards. A visual novel is an interactive production with a different kind of scene, not a fourth medium.

What kind of interactive?

clipscutbranch map

built · driftedwhat shipped
  • Built as drawn: CHOOSE asks which interactive, each kind with its plate, and Visual novel writes the visual-novel kind.
  • No TEXT or ADVANCE default: the line always shows in its box, and a beat moves on with a tap until its Beat card says otherwise. RATE is hidden, since a visual novel plays pictures.
Binding · turn 174 Visual novel — an interactive story told in pictures, text and voices, chosen at the CHOOSE door, authored as beats on the scene page, read in 156’s player (adds a kind to 113’s door; reuses 145, 156 and 157)

Binding — the kind. An illustrated story is medium: video, kind: visual-novel, reached only by CHOOSE → Visual novel (174a). productionShape reads it as branching and as dispatching images, the pairing the legacy stills kind already has for images. Everything keyed on isBranching therefore comes free: routing, the branch map, findings, walk evidence, preview and endings. The on-screen name is Visual novel, the form’s own name, which matches the kind’s id; its line (Pictures, text and voices. Read at your own pace, then choose.) explains it to anyone who does not know the genre. Not Illustrated: that word already names an art direction, which an interactive movie can wear, and a story’s page illustrations. The other card is Interactive movie (Scenes play as video. Choose at the end of each.), the production that exists today, which changes in nothing but its name on this step. A label names what the viewer does, never a medium’s technique (Moving pictures, drawn first, said neither). The step keeps the name field and its defaults, and adds two more: TEXT (Box, or Captions) and ADVANCE (On tap, or After the voice).

Binding — a beat is a shot. A beat is a shot that covers one script block. An action block is narration and a dialogue block is its speaker’s line (174b). built · drifted#/w/:worldId/p/:prodId/scenes/:sceneId · visual novelchecked 2026-09-27
174b in the master →

A scene of a visual novel is a list of beats. A beat is one picture and one line: narration, which the narrator reads, or a character’s line, read in that character’s voice. On disk a beat is a shot, and the line is the script block the shot covers, so the scene page, the cast, the Stage and the takes are the ones already built. What changes is what a row shows: the line and whose it is, whether it is voiced, and how it moves on. The scene ends in its choices, which the branch map owns.
