  • SPEC-042 / PR 875: a page, not a modal. Providers holds credentials; AI models holds models by kind then supplier. Sample clips on the card are issue 876.
Binding · turn 124 Settings is a page, and a model is something you can see (supersedes SPEC-034’s panel and model-row rules)

Binding. Settings is a page, not a panel. It keeps the app chrome, the rail sits flush left, and the scrim, the card, the shadow and the close × all go. This supersedes turn 112’s 90% dialog and turn 110’s 1088 × 680. A modal promises to put you back where you were and this one never did — its close went to /worlds from wherever you opened it. Leaving Settings returns you to the screen you came from, and the way out is the chrome’s own gear and the back gesture, not a control of the panel’s.

Binding. A model is drawn as a card only where a picture is a fact. Images and video, wherever they are — a keyed service’s models and an engine’s recipes alike. Everything else stays a row: language, text-to-speech, speech-to-text, music, components, engines, keys. A card over a language model is a box with the row’s words in it and more space spent saying them. 124a draws both in one pane, which is the case that proves the rule.

Binding. The card adds the picture and no words. Every fact it carries is the fact its row carried — name, capability, price or size, the switch, the state, the refusal clause — in the same spelling, from the same projection. Nothing is written for the card: no summary, no strapline, no quality claim. recommended is drawn because localPreference already names it; a best quality ribbon has nothing behind it and is not drawn.

Binding. Bands, in pixels: frame 152 (16:9 at 270 wide), name 18, meta 16, foot 28, pad 10/12/12. Every element the band pins is box-sizing:border-box. No action means no band — a keyed model’s switch is on the picture, so its card ends at the meta line rather than reserving 28px for a control it does not have. A refusal’s clause is the one thing allowed to wrap, to two lines: a measured shortfall truncated to this machine has 1… is the half a reader needed. Every foot that is drawn is the same height, so a wrapping row does not end ragged.

Binding. The grid holds at two, and the columns beside it fold first. Three-up at the page’s pane width, wrapping; as the window narrows the rail and the provider list give up their width before the grid gives up a column (124d, 860 wide: rail 146, list 186, cards 226). One card per line is a row that costs 127px of height, so the grid never draws it.

Binding. A pane of rows keeps a reading column, 760px. This is the one thing the panel was doing right by accident: at full page width a label and its value sit at opposite ends of 1100px and the eye has to cross the screen to pair them (124e). A grid pane takes the full width, because a card carries its own facts inside its own 270px.

Binding. A sample is a shipped file, one per model, and optional. 16:9, at most 4s, at most 400 KB, H.264 .mp4 beside a .jpg poster of its first frame, keyed by model id. The poster is what is drawn; the clip plays muted and looping only under the pointer or focus, one at a time, and never under prefers-reduced-motion. A model with a poster and no clip is complete. A model with neither draws a neutral plate and loses nothing else (124c, no clip) — so the manifest never waits on art to ship a model.

Binding. The state rules of turn 112 survive the container. A dot only where something warns; ready and a switch that is on say what a green dot would have said. A transfer draws its percentage over the picture and its figures in the foot. And turn 112’s D8 distinction holds on a card exactly as on a row: a declared unsupported recedes, because nobody can act on it, while a measured insufficient keeps full weight and its figures (124c) — a smaller model or a bigger card answers it.

Binding. A card switched off recedes. The row already muted an off model’s name; the card takes that to the whole tile at .55. This is not turn 112’s dimming rule being broken: off is neither a fit verdict nor a row state, it is the switch beside it, and a wall of pictures at equal weight is exactly the reading problem the dimming was for.

Binding. The pane’s footnote goes. a model switched off appears in no picker and cannot be a routing default · a default already pointing at one is flagged in General, never re-routed for you is a paragraph explaining a switch, which turn 69 forbids and which no card makes truer. The refusal it anticipates already has a place: on the default it flags, in General.

builtwhat shipped
  • Kinds, then suppliers; the working prototype behind it is settings-models.html.
Binding · turn 125 Providers holds the credential, AI models holds the models — grouped by what they make, then by who supplies them (supersedes turn 124; amends SPEC-034 R-1, R-5)

Binding. Two surfaces. Providers holds credentials — a key, a sign-in, an engine’s source and address — and never a model. AI models holds every model, cloud and local. This supersedes turn 124 and amends SPEC-034 R-1 and R-5, whose single Providers surface carried both. Providers says exactly one thing about models: a count and the way there (8 fal models, 5 of them on) — never a list, and never a control that belongs to the other surface.

Binding. The remedy for a missing credential is rendered on AI models, never as a route to Providers. This is the rule the split has to clear: SPEC-033 R-7 requires a screen to render the owning surface’s control rather than navigate to it, and turn 112 merged these two surfaces precisely because Cloud AI filtered by a switch it could not reach and shipped an Open Providers button instead. Here the switch lives wholly on AI models, and a provider that cannot be reached states it once at its section heading with the fix there — Add a key, Sign in (125a, 125c). If that ever becomes a button that navigates, the split has regressed and must be undone.

Binding. Three columns, on both surfaces: the settings rail, then what you are choosing among, then the detail. On AI models the second column is the kinds, grouped Cloud above and On this machine below, each kind with its count. On Providers it is the providers, grouped Services you connect and Engines you run — turn 112’s words, unchanged. Every kind is present at once rather than found by scrolling, which is what turn 124’s single column cost.

Binding. A half is drawn as a level, not typeset as one. Cloud and On this machine take a rule above the group, an icon beside the label, the weight and colour of the foreground where the kinds under them stay muted, and the kinds indented 12px past the heading. Four quiet devices. Not a larger size and not capitals — the first fights the pane title, the second is the tracked-out eyebrow turn 69 spent a sweep removing.

Binding. Within a kind, models are grouped by who supplies them, and the group heading is the provider: its mark, its name, and on the right either its count or its remedy. Stated once, at the heading — never repeated on every tile, which is where turn 124 put it and where it was the quietest thing on the card.

Binding. The tile, measured: 282 wide, picture 158 (16:9 at the 280 inside the border), body 68, total 228; three up in a 886 pane with a 20 gutter, wrapping. The gutter is the point — turn 124’s gapless sheet was a fine object and a poor list, and this screen is read one model at a time. A tile that can be switched carries a switch; one that cannot carries its state in words (Ready, 9 of 34 GB) and no switch at all, because a control that does nothing is worse than none.

Binding. A kind with nothing to show keeps the same three columns and becomes rows (125c). Text-to-Speech, Speech-to-Text, Voice clone, Music and Language have no picture, and a card over one is a box with the row’s words in it. Each voice row carries a play control: a speaking sample is that model’s equivalent of a picture, and the same sentence is spoken by every one of them so the comparison is of voices and not of scripts.

Binding. A sample is a shipped file, one per visual model, and optional. 16:9, at most 4s, at most 400 KB, H.264 .mp4 beside a .jpg poster of its first frame, keyed by model id. The poster is what is drawn; the clip plays muted and looping only under the pointer or focus, one at a time, and never under prefers-reduced-motion. A model with neither draws a plain plate and loses nothing else, so the manifest never waits on art. Carried unchanged from turn 124.

Binding. Off is a ghost of the picture at .42, greyed: you can still see what you are declining. Turn 112’s D8 distinction survives the container — a declared unsupported recedes because nobody can act on it, while a measured shortfall keeps its figures at full weight (Wants 20 GB, this card has 12), because a smaller model or a bigger card answers it.

Binding. A row action is a button with an icon and its verb. Icon-only was drawn first and reverted: it made the rows tidy and every action a guess, and Test again is not a glyph anyone knows. The icon makes an action findable at a glance, the word makes it certain, and the visible label is the accessible name — so no tooltip carries it a second time. The row already names what is being changed, so the button does not repeat it: Change, never Change source. Destructive stays quiet at rest and takes the signal colour only on hover; the weight belongs on the confirm, not on a settings row nobody is touching.

Binding. A provider carries its own mark, bundled, never fetched at runtime. Every mark sits on one light plate in both themes: half of them are a black glyph on transparency and would disappear against a dark pane. Voxa carries the Arke mark — it is our own engine, and the mark is what says so. A provider that serves no mark keeps a monogram in the same 22px slot; nothing in the layout depends on having one.

Binding. The capability words are turn 110’s, unchanged: Images, Video, Text-to-Speech, Speech-to-Text, Voice clone, Music, Language. They are the words both surfaces share and the words the rail is built from. Plainer substitutes were drafted for these frames and cut: one vocabulary, or the two screens drift.

Destructive stays quiet at rest and takes the signal colour only on hover; the weight belongs on the confirm, not on a settings row nobody is touching.

Binding. A provider carries its own mark, bundled, never fetched at runtime. Every mark sits on one light plate in both themes: half of them are a black glyph on transparency and would disappear against a dark pane. Voxa carries the Arke mark — it is our own engine, and the mark is what says so. A provider that serves no mark keeps a monogram in the same 22px slot; nothing in the layout depends on having one.

Binding. The capability words are turn 110’s, unchanged: Images, Video, Text-to-Speech, Speech-to-Text, Voice clone, Music, Language. They are the words both surfaces share and the words the rail is built from. Plainer substitutes were drafted for these frames and cut: one vocabulary, or the two screens drift.

Binding · turn 136 Activity is a panel, not a page — a bell in the chrome opens it over the screen you are on, with everything the page held inside it and two things the page never had: the app’s own news, first, and the spend alert as a row (retires the Activity page of 26a; amends 42b and 79)

Binding. The panel replaces the page. The bell opens a panel over the current screen; /activity is retired and resolves to Home with the panel open; a Windows notification’s click and a receipt’s Activity action open it in place. Everything the page held is inside: Needs you, Running, Earlier by day, Spend, drift, the founding build’s not-landed rows with Run and Run all, provider calls, delete with its second press. Nothing about Activity leaves the screen you are on. It closes on an outside press, on Escape, and on any action of its own that navigates.

Binding. Three tabs, What’s new first. What’s new, Inbox, Spend, in that order. The panel opens on Inbox while anything needs you and on What’s new otherwise, so the news is met on a quiet day and never stands between a person and a decision; a Windows notification’s click and a receipt’s Activity action open Inbox regardless. A tab’s label carries its count: Inbox’s is the Needs-you count, What’s new’s is what has not been read (an update waiting counts once), and Spend carries none. The status line under the tabs is the panel’s, not the tab’s: the running and needs-you figures on the left, the scope on the right (this world · all worlds, the active one --foreground), defaulting to the open world as SPEC-014 R-1 has it. What’s new has no scope and no status line.

Binding. Needs you leads. The Inbox orders Needs you, then Running, then Earlier by day (TODAY, YESTERDAY, 2 DAYS AGO, to seven days) — the page’s order reversed, because the panel is opened to act and the page was opened to watch. Class before recency within Needs you (SPEC-014 R-5) is unchanged, and nothing here can be dismissed: a row leaves when the decision exists (SPEC-014 D1). A spend alert that fired is a Needs-you row, class 2 beside blocked work: Over the spend alert, the figures on the mono line, and Spend as its one action. It leaves when the rolling total drops below the line or the line moves. A row’s actions are the page’s, offered only where the state permits them (SPEC-014 R-13): beside the text for Running and Earlier, on their own line for Needs you.

Binding. The bell is a bell. The chrome’s Activity control draws a bell in place of the pulse it wore since 26a — the ordinary glyph for a notification drawer, which is what it now opens. Same 13px box, same title, same dots, same place in the 42b order; swept across every screen of both documents and the app’s own icon, so no drawn screen carries the old glyph.

Binding. Two dots on the bell, one meaning each. --warning while Needs you holds anything; --foreground when something came back since the panel was last opened or a release is unread; nothing otherwise. Warning wins when both apply, and the title names which. Opening the panel clears the foreground dot and nothing else — the warning dot clears only with the queue. No count is drawn on the bell; the counts are on the tabs.

Binding. What is remembered. Two facts, and nothing per row: when the Inbox was last opened, and the last release read. Both live in the app’s settings file beside the theme and the background-notification preference, so every window and the dev browser agree. The queue itself stays computed.

Binding. What’s new ships with the build. Each release carries a card — a picture, a title, the notes, a date — kept in the repository beside the release and copied into the build; the last eight ride along, so the tab is a history and not one card. No feed is fetched: the tab says nothing the installer did not bring, except one card at the top for an update that is waiting, drawn from what the updater already fetched with its check. That card carries the update’s own controls — Download, then Install and restart and Install when I close, with the download’s percent while it runs — and About keeps its row (SPEC-016 R-17). Binding · turn 151 An Arke account in the chrome — the person’s picture at the end of the bar, a menu under it, and a door in when no one is signed in (Arke cloud, ahead of its spec)

Binding. The account is the last control in the chrome’s right group — after the gear, before the desktop’s native window controls, whose 138 stays clear as it does for the rest. It is the one thing in the bar about the person rather than the screen, and every product puts it at the end. Signed in it is the person’s picture, 18 round in the 26×22 slot, or their initials on the secondary tint when there is no picture — the Avatar component’s two forms at a smaller size. Signed out it is the person glyph, drawn like the bell and the gear. Signed out it carries nothing: no dot, no badge, no pulse, no tooltip that sells. The app is whole without an account (SPEC-025: it runs on a machine with no network and no account), so the control is a door, not a notice. The one dot it ever wears is warning, for a session that has expired, and it means what the bell’s means: something wants you.

Binding. Pressed, it opens a menu, never a page. 300 wide, right-aligned to the control, 6 under the bar; the card colour, the border, 11 radius, shadow-lg — the bench’s session menu (68b), not the Activity panel. role="menu", and the role is honoured: the arrows move, Escape and an outside press close it, focus goes back to the control. Three bands, rules between them. The person: picture 36, name, address. The facts and the doors, rows of 36 in turn 149’s grammar — label, value, the action at the end: Plan with the plan’s name and Upgrade (or Manage, once there is a plan to manage), then Account. Sign out on a band of its own. Anything that leaves the app wears the ↗ glyph and opens the system browser; the app draws no billing, no profile form, no card field. Nothing that lives in Settings is repeated here.

Binding. Signed out, the same menu holds one title and two buttons: Arke account, Sign in as the primary, Create account as the outline, both full width and both wearing the ↗ glyph, because both leave the app. Sign-in is a browser handoff, as vendor sign-in already is (SPEC-030): the app opens Arke cloud in the system browser and waits, and never draws a password field. While it waits the buttons give way to one line, waiting for the browser with the spinner, and Cancel. No pitch above the buttons and no sentence under the title: a screen labels, it does not explain (turn 137).

Binding. The words. The thing is the Arke account — never Sign-in, which Settings already uses for vendor sign-in, and never login. The states are three, in the state-word voice of turn 149: waiting for the browser · session expired (warning, with the dot on the picture and Sign in ↗ as the row’s action) · offline (in the plan row, in place of the action; the picture stays, because offline is not the person’s to fix). The plan’s name is a badge of the outline kind: Free today, and whatever the paid tier is called. Nothing local is gated by the account: every screen, provider and world works signed out exactly as it does today, and the account adds Arke cloud on top.

What’s new

CHAPTER 07 OF 24

The counting of bells

Read the chapter
drafting1,900 wordssaved

Maren counted the bells the way her mother had taught her, on the fingers of the left hand only, so the right stayed free for the rope. Six, and the tide not yet called. She let the seventh go by without a finger for it.

The Vigil was cold at slack water. It was always cold at slack water; the stone gave back whatever the sea had left in it overnight, and what the sea left was never warmth. She stood with her back to the harbour and her face to the drowned city and waited for the water to decide.

It did not decide. The seventh bell rang again — not the echo of the sixth, which she knew, but its own note, lower, wet at the edges. Nobody had called it. She had not called it. The rope hung slack in her hand and the bell rang a third time anyway.

“That is not how it works,” she said, aloud, to the water, because there was no one else to say it to and the rule wanted saying. The bells answered a called tide. Everyone knew that. It was the first thing a bell-keeper learned and the last thing they were allowed to forget.

The city under the water did not care what everyone knew. It rang a fourth time, and now she could hear where it was coming from — not the harbour bells at all, but somewhere out past the Vigil’s edge, past the last of the marker posts, where the ledger said there was nothing but silt.

She put a finger down for it. Seven. Then, because her hand was shaking and she did not want to look at it, she put the rope down too.

A row in Chapters is a destination at story/chapters/:chapterId, and that route folds the rail by default exactly as scenes/:sceneId does in the shipped rail, because the manuscript is a workspace (turn 82’s fold), and the width is the person’s afterwards: the rail’s own control remembers it for the session. New chapter is a press, not a form: it creates Untitled live and opens it, the shape SPEC-036 R-37 gave scenes, on the create-chapter command the coordinator already answers. The screen is called Chapters, the rail’s word; Chapter tree was a title nobody pressed.

Binding. The body is fetched on open and never carried on the summary. ChapterSummary stays body-free, as its own comment says, and a novel is the reason: eighty thousand words on every snapshot broadcast is the bundle turned into the book. Opening asks the coordinator for the file and gets body and version back; the editor holds the version it read, the save carries it, and the local draft is dropped on the next snapshot rather than on dispatch — the Bible’s three-writer rule in bible.tsx, applied unchanged. A save refused for a moved version leaves the text where it is and lets the snapshot say so, which is what every direct-authoring save here already does.

Binding. Typing saves in place after 1200ms. No proposal and no version cut, per SPEC-012 R-5; saveChapter already restamps words, so the tree and the dashboard follow the prose without a second count. The foot says Saved · v2 · 1,900 words and nothing else, and Markdown source is the Bible’s toggle behind the Bible’s gate. The manuscript is set at a reading measure of 640 inside a centre of 983, with a side of 250; the dock is 331 and the folded rail 46, the build’s numbers, so the three columns are 123a’s three columns.

Binding. Read the chapter reads the saved record, a paragraph at a time. A chapter arm joins ProseReadSource — { of: "chapter", productionId, chapterId } — and because the body is not in the bundle the resolver reads the file rather than staying a pure function of the bundle, the way the Bible’s section read does. It is a page read (issue 859): the screen names its blocks, one per paragraph, in order, and the words never travel. Unsaved typing is not what is heard. The press waits out the autosave before it asks, so the voice and the page cannot disagree about what the chapter says.

Binding. Draws on is shown, not inferred. The side lists the sheets and canon on the chapter’s draws, each a link to its record, and says Draws on nothing yet when there are none. Nothing reads the prose for names in this slice: a novel’s sentences are not @ mentions (SPEC-012 R-9 is a shot’s rule), and guessing would put a wrong sheet beside a chapter with the confidence of a fact. Arke sets draws when it drafts — production-chapter already carries it — and the author changes it in the thread. Earlier versions is the Bible’s list: one line per version, Restore makes a new one.

Binding. Arke’s column is the production thread, about this chapter. No new entry context. The dock enters { kind: "production" } with a subjectPrefix of About chapter 07:, so a draft asked for from Develop and one asked for here are one conversation and one card (issue 714), and a chapter drafted before this screen existed is decided on it. While a draft waits the editor locks — the scene workspace’s rule for a staged scene — and the manuscript shows the draft in the prose’s place under a band that names it and counts it; the card in the thread holds Accept and Discard and the page holds neither. Accept writes the file; Discard returns the saved text. Talking writes nothing else, and the line under the composer says so in the dock’s own words.

Binding. The target is a band, never a sentence. targetLength is a free string; the band draws only when it parses to a number of words, reads 21,400 of 80,000 words, and sums words off the summaries. When it does not parse, the count stands alone. Rows in Chapters are a band of 46, box-sizing:border-box, and carry number, title, version, then words or status — a chapter with no words says its status, which is the shipped rule. No state on either screen explains itself; the reasons are here.

Binding — planned controls are absent, not disabled. A control whose service has not landed is not in the build: no struck Sound chip waiting for 1334, no greyed Design a voice waiting for 1332, no Saved filter with nothing behind it. It appears when the coordinator reports the capability behind it — a reader that declares sounds, a provider that can design, a voice library that holds saved voices — so the structure ships once and each issue turns its controls on by reporting what it can do. A disabled control with no way to enable it is the prototype’s dead affordance, and the house does not ship one. What this turn builds now: the head, the block panel, the searchable narrator dialog with the switch’s costs, provider names, and the widths below.

Binding — the head names the reading. The chapter’s view row is 155e’s: the Manuscript · Audiobook seg, then the reading as a menu button in mono — Performed · Charon, the reading in --muted-foreground and the narrator in the foreground, a chevron — then Play and Read the chapter · N blocks · $X at the right. Play is there whenever one block has a made take and gives way to Stop and Skip while it plays; the priced read is the primary while anything is left to make. The menu, 248, is headed READING · WHOLE BOOK: Narrator, Performed, Cast as radio items with their data (one voice, notes, 7 voices), a rule, and Narrator…, which opens 165c. Binding — the block panel is words, chips and one row of buttons. The title is Block 16 · Odile Sarn in --type-label semibold, sentence case, with no tracking — not two columns of letter-spaced capitals — and under it one mono line naming the reader by its voice and role: read by Charon · narrator, · performed under Performed, read by Anna · Maren Kest under Cast. Delivery is six pill chips 24 high that wrap, the chosen one filled, a radiogroup named Delivery; what the reader cannot do is struck with the reason as the title. The marker list shows a plate and the words it covers verbatim — the span as the block has it, never wrapped in quotation marks of its own, so “Whoever cut the tenth key, cannot become ““Whoever cut the tenth key,””; a point names its neighbour, before and the words. Under it the add buttons — Marker · Pause · Breath · Emphasis, and Sound when 1334 reports it — each a 24-high dashed pill holding a plus and one word that never part (white-space: nowrap); the row wraps between buttons, never inside one. Each is named for what it adds (Add pause). A take row is v2 · 0:04 · George · Kokoro: the version, the running time, the voice and the reader’s name from the catalogue.

Binding — a provider is a name and a place, never an id. Every audiobook surface names a reader by the catalogue’s words: the provider’s display name and where it runs — Kokoro · this machine, Google · cloud, Mistral · cloud — and, where a model is the reader, the reader’s name (Gemini Flash, Eleven v3, Voxtral). mistral · voxtral-mini-tts is an id and is never on screen: not in the dialog’s rows, the Voices panel, the door’s chips, the take rows, the confirm press or the price sheet. Binding · turn 146 The audiobook — a kept take for every block, direction beside the prose, and the book out as chapter files (story mode, slice 7; extends 126a, 130a and 131a; amends 130’s Voices panel)

Binding — a kept take for every block. An audiobook is the story production’s third export, beside .docx and EPUB (131a); it is not a medium and not a second entity model. Its working state is one take per block, the block being 130’s: each paragraph split at its cast lines into narration and lines, in order, addressed and never carried as words. Under Narrator every block is the narrator’s; under Cast a line is its speaker’s, the sheet’s assignment (SPEC-011 R-14), and narration the narrator’s. A paragraph that is a scene break — the marks the manuscript export reads as one — is a separator, not a block: no take, no state, two seconds of silence in the file. A block whose rendered text — the words with the reader’s tags, phrase and cues already in it — is longer than the reader’s prompt cap is made in parts, each part bounded after rendering, split at sentence ends, where one sentence is itself too long at a word, and where one word is itself too long at a character; each part a request, joined on this machine into the one kept take, as local speech already splits a long section; the sidecar records the parts. A take is production media: a file under artifacts/ with a sidecar naming the chapter, the paragraph and occurrence, the hash of the block’s text, the voice and its reader, the sheet version the voice was assigned at (SPEC-013 R-18), the direction’s hash, the format and the cost — the record a generated performance keeps, so review, A/B and purge already know its shape. It is listed on Artifacts, borrowable by the Cut, never in .index/, and never in the speech cache, which stays the table read’s and the voiced read’s. The chapter’s audiobook record lives beside its cast at productions/<production>/.audiobook/<chapter>.json — the direction per block and the take chosen for it, keyed to the chapter’s version and the hash of its prose — unversioned, no track of the gate’s, carried by export, written through the store’s ownership-checked path so a run that finishes after the world’s claim was lost writes nothing.

Binding — direction beside the prose, never in it. The words are the author’s and go out as .docx and EPUB untouched, so nothing of the reading is typed into a paragraph: no (whisper), no (break). A block’s direction is SPEC-011’s cadence plan kept on the record and keyed to the block’s text hash — one of the six deliveries (measured · whispered · breaking · cold · warm · urgent), an optional phrase of at most 60 characters (to the water, flat) for the readers that take language, speed within the plan’s 0.7–1.2, and cues — a pause, short or long; a breath; an emphasis on a span — at positions in the block’s text. The phrase is an amendment to the cadence contract, not a side path: the plan gains a phrase field, the capabilities a phrase declaration, and mapCadence renders it and reports it with the other controls (SPEC-047 R-6, R-7). The reader renders it: a tag on the rows that have one, a bracket phrase on Fish and Breeze, an instruction where the row declares one, nothing on Voxtral. The block panel says per control what this reader does, in one clause — phrase · best-effort, Voxtral reads as recorded — and a delivery the reader cannot express is refused on the control, never made neutral in silence. A changed wording drops the block’s direction, since the plan was authored for other words, and the block is stale. Direct this chapter is a dock prompt: Arke proposes a direction for every block in 129’s discipline — JSON, every block addressed, deliveries within the six, cues at positions that exist, phrases within the cap, and every control checked against the row of the block’s effective reader, the assigned voice or the narrator it falls to, so a whisper asked of Kokoro, which reads measured or urgent, is dropped and counted rather than accepted into a direction the read could only flag — as one card in the thread, accepted whole or discarded; accepting writes the record and nothing else. Prose is edited in Manuscript; the Audiobook view shows it as blocks and does not edit it.

Binding — one book, two readings, and nothing falls back in silence. The door’s Narrator · Cast is the book’s choice, kept on the production and read by every chapter; the narrator is the app’s (turn 70), the cast’s voices are the sheets’. Under Cast, a speaker with no assigned voice, or whose voice’s provider or model cannot synthesise now, is said before anything is made — no voice · narrator, voice unavailable · narrator, in warning, on the door’s voices row and in the chapter’s Voices panel — and the block is then made in the narrator’s voice as a take whose sidecar records it. A file never carries a substitution the door did not show — and that includes a line whose speaker the cast cannot name: under Cast a run needs a cast that is current, cast against the chapter’s version and prose, so a chapter with no cast, an unreadable one, or one the prose has moved under says so on its row (not cast, cast moved · cast again) and is refused by the run until it is cast again, and a line a current cast counts ambiguous is disclosed on the door’s voices row (unattributed · 2 lines · narrator) before it is read in the narrator’s voice. Under Narrator no cast is needed. Changing the choice, or a sheet’s voice, leaves every take standing, marks the blocks whose reader changed stale, and re-checks each such block’s direction against the new reader’s row, dropping what it cannot express and saying how many — a whisper accepted for Anna is not carried to George, whose row reads measured or urgent, to be flagged on every retry.

Binding — four states, and a batch that resumes. A block is not made, made, stale (its text, its reader or its direction changed since the take) or flagged (the make failed, the reader refused the direction, or a check found the take wrong); the dot beside the block is the state, the foot counts them, the door’s row sums them — 22 of 26 made · 1 flagged, moved · 3 of 24 stale, read · 24:10 — and a chapter with no prose has no blocks at all — no title block either — says planned as Chapters does, is skipped by Read the book and never exports. The chapter’s title is its first block, Chapter 7 · The counting of bells, read by the narrator under either reading, with a state and a take like any other. Read the chapter and Read the book make every block that is not made — not made, stale and flagged alike, so a failed block is retried rather than left to hold the export — in reading order, as queued jobs keyed by world, production and chapter as continuity’s runs are: replayed to a renderer that connects, stopped through the harness’s interrupt, aborted when the world closes, the takes already made left standing. They are priced once by the character for cloud voices and confirmed once, naming each cloud voice and its provider and where the words go (SPEC-012 R-47’s token); a local voice and a take already made cost nothing and say nothing, and a press whose blocks would cost nothing asks nothing. A stop leaves what was made; the next press makes only what is missing. A local voice is one job at a time on this machine, so the row says reading… 12 of 38 with Stop in the press’s place, and a book on IndexTTS is an overnight run the door reports rather than hides. A line already in the speech cache under the cache’s own identity — the same text, provider, model and voice id, which is how the cache names a file — and with no direction is adopted as a take without a call; the same voice id through another reader is a miss, as a reader change is a stale block.

Binding — one player, and no timeline. The chapter’s player is the table read’s, as 130’s is: it plays the made takes in order, the manuscript marks the block sounding, the head names the reader and the count (Maren Kest · 5 of 26) and holds Stop and Skip; a block not made is skipped and counted; a press on a block’s dot plays that take alone; the read stops when the page is left. There is no timeline: the manuscript is the order, and a bed under a chapter is the Cut’s work on the exported file.

Binding — a chapter exports whole or not at all. Export on the door is a sheet in the manuscript export’s shape: Chapter files (one file a chapter, MP3 192 kbps CBR at 44.1 kHz, or WAV 44.1 kHz 16-bit) or Book (one M4B, AAC, a chapter marker per chapter from its title) — the format row follows the choice, MP3 192 kbps · WAV under the first and M4B alone under the second, so the sheet cannot describe a file it will not make; Retail — RMS between −23 and −18 dBFS, true peak at −3 dBTP, noise floor under −60 dB RMS, 0.5 s of room tone at the head and 2 s at the tail, and no chapter file longer than 120 minutes, a longer chapter split at a paragraph — or, when one paragraph’s take is itself longer than that, between the parts it was made from — and numbered 07-1, 07-2; the book is one file whatever its length, since the cap is a retailer’s rule for chapter files and a book is not what a retailer takes — or As made. Assembly is a rule, not a control: the title block’s take opens the file, 0.8 s stands between paragraphs, 0.4 s between narration and a line, 2 s at a scene break. A chapter exports only when every block, the title included, is made and current; a chapter with a block not made, stale or flagged is left out and counted on the sheet, and Read the rest · 9 chapters · $0.94 is the dashed door beside the count, in Play lines’ shape (SPEC-044 R-33), so the export itself never makes a take and never calls a provider. Rendered locally by the bundled ffmpeg with no provider call (SPEC-013 R-19), staged so a cancel leaves nothing named (R-21), progress on the sheet; the files land under <world>/exports/<slug>-audiobook-<date>-<id>/ and Show in folder opens the folder on the host. A render is not publication (SPEC-038 R-36).

Binding — sizes, the rail and the copy. Binding — a kept take for every block. An audiobook is the story production’s third export, beside .docx and EPUB (131a); it is not a medium and not a second entity model. Its working state is one take per block, the block being 130’s: each paragraph split at its cast lines into narration and lines, in order, addressed and never carried as words. Under Narrator every block is the narrator’s; under Cast a line is its speaker’s, the sheet’s assignment (SPEC-011 R-14), and narration the narrator’s. A paragraph that is a scene break — the marks the manuscript export reads as one — is a separator, not a block: no take, no state, two seconds of silence in the file. A block whose rendered text — the words with the reader’s tags, phrase and cues already in it — is longer than the reader’s prompt cap is made in parts, each part bounded after rendering, split at sentence ends, where one sentence is itself too long at a word, and where one word is itself too long at a character; each part a request, joined on this machine into the one kept take, as local speech already splits a long section; the sidecar records the parts. A take is production media: a file under artifacts/ with a sidecar naming the chapter, the paragraph and occurrence, the hash of the block’s text, the voice and its reader, the sheet version the voice was assigned at (SPEC-013 R-18), the direction’s hash, the format and the cost — the record a generated performance keeps, so review, A/B and purge already know its shape. It is listed on Artifacts, borrowable by the Cut, never in .index/, and never in the speech cache, which stays the table read’s and the voiced read’s. The chapter’s audiobook record lives beside its cast at productions/<production>/.audiobook/<chapter>.json — the direction per block and the take chosen for it, keyed to the chapter’s version and the hash of its prose — unversioned, no track of the gate’s, carried by export, written through the store’s ownership-checked path so a run that finishes after the world’s claim was lost writes nothing.

Binding — direction beside the prose, never in it. The words are the author’s and go out as .docx and EPUB untouched, so nothing of the reading is typed into a paragraph: no (whisper), no (break). A block’s direction is SPEC-011’s cadence plan kept on the record and keyed to the block’s text hash — one of the six deliveries (measured · whispered · breaking · cold · warm · urgent), an optional phrase of at most 60 characters (to the water, flat) for the readers that take language, speed within the plan’s 0.7–1.2, and cues — a pause, short or long; a breath; an emphasis on a span — at positions in the block’s text. The phrase is an amendment to the cadence contract, not a side path: the plan gains a phrase field, the capabilities a phrase declaration, and mapCadence renders it and reports it with the other controls (SPEC-047 R-6, R-7). The reader renders it: a tag on the rows that have one, a bracket phrase on Fish and Breeze, an instruction where the row declares one, nothing on Voxtral. The block panel says per control what this reader does, in one clause — phrase · best-effort, Voxtral reads as recorded — and a delivery the reader cannot express is refused on the control, never made neutral in silence. A changed wording drops the block’s direction, since the plan was authored for other words, and the block is stale. Binding — one book, two readings, and nothing falls back in silence. The door’s Narrator · Cast is the book’s choice, kept on the production and read by every chapter; the narrator is the app’s (turn 70), the cast’s voices are the sheets’. In the Audiobook view the 70px mark column of 146b becomes a 96px speaker column holding a chip: an 8px dot and the name in var(--type-label), 22px high, ellipsed. The chip names who speaks the block by the cast — under Narrator as under Cast, since who speaks is the prose’s fact and who reads is the Voices panel’s. Narration and the title are narrator in --neutral-400; a speaker with a sheet takes a colour; a name no sheet carries is a dashed dot in --muted-foreground. A line’s block carries a 2px rule and a 7% tint in its speaker’s colour; narration carries neither, so the lines stand out of the prose without a label. Colours are a new token set, --voice-1 to --voice-6, one pair for light and one for dark, given to the book’s speakers in the order of their first line in the book and repeated past six, so a speaker keeps one colour in every chapter; the narrator never takes one, and --success, --warning and --destructive are never a speaker’s, since the state dot uses them. Beside the state dot a 44px marks cell shows how the kept take was made: a waveform for a voice, a microphone for a recording, nothing when there is no take. The row over the blocks is a filter — Everyone, Narrator, then each speaker in colour order, each with its block or line count — and choosing one dims every other block to 40% and makes Play play that speaker’s made takes alone (Odile Sarn · 2 of 4); the choice is not kept past the page.

Binding — the cast is derived, and a correction outlives it. 130 made the cast of lines derived and never authored; this amends it. The record at productions/<production>/.voices/<chapter>.json gains pins: authored corrections kept beside the derived lines, each { paragraph, quote, occurrence, speaker } where speaker is a sheet id, a name no sheet carries, or narration — this span is not a line. A press on a block’s chip opens the speaker menu, 236px: a search, IN THIS CHAPTER with Narration first and the chapter’s speakers, then CAST with the rest of the world’s sheets, each with its voice as data (no voice); a name typed that no sheet carries is offered as itself. Words selected inside a narration block open the same menu for the selection and make it a line: the selection must sit in one paragraph, cross no line, and hold between 1 and 600 characters, 130’s cap; otherwise the menu does not open. A pin is verified as a derived line is — the quote found exactly once at its occurrence in its paragraph, whitespace folded — and applied over the derived lines: a derived line that overlaps a pin gives way. Cast again keeps every pin that still verifies and derives around it; a pin whose words have moved is dropped and counted in the stamp (1 correction lost), never re-placed by guess. A pinned block carries a pin in its marks cell; the stamp counts pins (cast · v4 · 10 lines · 1 set by you). A pin changes who reads the block, so a take made for the old speaker goes stale by 146’s rule. A pin is written through the cast record’s ownership-checked path; it touches no sheet, no world track and no gate. The cast of a chapter with pins is current exactly as before: against the version and the hash of the prose.

Binding — a take is made or recorded. 146’s take gains a source: made, as before, or recorded, an audio file the author brings. Upload sits in the block’s Takes, and a file dropped on a block opens the same dialog, 540px: the block’s words in its speaker’s colour, the file with its waveform and technical line, the checks, the performer and the rights, Keep as take. WAV, FLAC, MP3 and M4A are read, one file a block, up to 10 minutes and 200 MB; the file is prepared through the audio foundation’s local path (issue 117) to the take format, 44.1 kHz mono, and no byte of it leaves the machine. The checks are the foundation’s QC report shown as data: loudness, peak and noise floor against Retail’s figures, and the words — a local transcript compared with the block’s text, match, 2 words differ, or words · unchecked where no local transcriber is present. A warning never refuses: a take with a noisy floor is kept and says so, and Retail export treats it as a take it must bring to profile. A hard incompatibility — undecodable, silent, over the limits — refuses in one clause on the file. Rights is required once a dialog, My voice · Authorized · Licensed, recorded as an AudioRightsEvent acknowledgement with a new scope recorded-take (an amendment to AudioRightsScopeSchema); the performer is the event’s performerRef, user-only, never in logs or a provider payload. A recorded take is production media as a made one is: a file under artifacts/ with a sidecar naming the chapter, paragraph and occurrence, the text hash, the source file’s hash and the prepared hash, the QC report and the acknowledgement id; its cost is nothing. It is chosen on the record as any take is, and it is current while the block’s text hash matches — a change of reader or of direction does not stale a recording, since neither made it; changed words do. A block whose chosen take is a current recording is never remade by Read the chapter or Read the book.

Binding — a speaker can be recorded. In the Voices panel a row is two lines, name and count over the reader, and each reader is a menu: the sheet’s voice, as 146 draws it, or Recorded, with an optional performer. Recorded is the book’s choice, kept on the audiobook book record beside reading as a list of sheet ids and narrator — an author may record their own narration — and never on the sheet, whose voice stays the voice every other read uses. Under Cast a recorded speaker’s block is made only by a recording: with no current recorded take it is awaiting, a fifth state beside 146’s four — the hollow dot with a microphone in the marks cell — counted in the foot and on the door’s row and voices (Odile Sarn · recorded · 2 awaiting). An awaiting block is left out of the run’s count and price, so Read the chapter · 5 blocks never promises a line it will not make, and it holds the export as a block not made does: a chapter exports whole. A made take kept for a block whose speaker becomes recorded stays in Takes and can be chosen by hand; the block reads awaiting until it is. Switching a speaker back to their voice makes their blocks without a current take not made, and the next read makes them.

Binding — lines out to a performer and back. A recorded speaker’s row opens a 680px sheet named for the speaker over a data line (31 lines · 9 chapters · 17 recorded · 14 awaiting). Script exports a PDF of the speaker’s lines in book order — Awaiting or All 31 — each with its id, the narration before it for context in grey, and its direction as a note: the delivery and the phrase, since direction is what a performer reads. A line’s id is CC-PPP-O: the chapter’s order, the paragraph and the occurrence in it, the address the cast already keeps (07-011-1). The script carries the chapter’s version and each line’s text hash. Add files takes many files at once; each is matched by the id in its name, then checked as one upload is. A file whose id names no line is refused (no line id); a file whose line’s words have changed since the script is refused (words changed), never kept against new words. Rows are file, line, check, in a 38 band; what passes or warns is ticked, what is refused is not and cannot be; the rights are given once for the batch. Keep 4 takes keeps the ticked files as recorded takes, one commit of records per chapter through the same ownership-checked path, and names nothing it did not keep.

Binding — markers direct inside a block, and still never touch the prose. 146 kept direction beside the words and refused tags typed into them; that stands. A marker is direction drawn in the Audiobook view at a place in the block’s text, and kept on the audiobook record: Manuscript shows none, and .docx and EPUB carry none. There are two kinds. A cue sits at a point — 146’s pause short or long, breath, and emphasis on a span — unchanged. A delivery marker is new: one of the six deliveries, or a phrase of at most 60 characters, over a span of the block’s text, amending the cadence contract with a cue kind delivery — { kind: "delivery", span: { from, to, text }, delivery?, phrase? }, at least one of the two — checked as emphasis is: exact span text, valid boundaries, position order, and no overlap with another delivery marker. The block’s own delivery is the reading outside every marker; a marker overrides it over its span and the block’s delivery resumes after. Markers and cues together stay within the plan’s 40. Placing one: select words and press [, or type [ at a caret — the Audiobook view has no text to edit, so the key opens the marker menu rather than typing — and choose; from a caret a delivery runs to the end of the sentence, a cue sits at the caret. The menu, 268px, is a search, DELIVERY as six chips, CUE as four, and Phrase…; what the block’s effective reader cannot do is struck with the reason as its hint (Kokoro reads measured or urgent), never accepted to be flagged later. On the page a marker is its word in brackets in mono, [whispered], on an 8% plate, and the span a delivery covers carries a dotted underline; a press on a marker opens the menu to change or remove it. The side lists the block’s markers and, as data, the text the reader is sent — [whispers] “I love you.” on a tag reader. The reader renders a delivery marker as 146 renders a block’s delivery, in place: an inline tag on the rows that have one (ElevenLabs v3, Fish, Breeze where the line is stated English), and on a row that carries delivery only through settings or an instruction, by making the block in parts split at the marker’s boundaries, each part with its own delivery, joined on this machine into the one take as 146’s parts are. A changed wording no longer drops a block’s direction whole: each marker whose span text is still found exactly once in the block is carried to its new place, and the rest are dropped and counted (2 markers dropped · words changed); the block is stale either way. Adding, changing or removing a marker makes the block stale. Direct this chapter proposes markers as it proposes cues, in 129’s discipline, each checked against the effective reader. Markers work under both readings; under Narrator the chips still name who speaks, so a whisper can be put on a line knowing whose line it is. A recorded speaker’s script prints its markers inline, [whispered] Not tonight., as the direction a performer reads.

Binding — the narrator performs the cast. The book’s reading gains a third value between the two 146 drew: Narrator · Performed · Cast, the door’s seg and AudiobookReadingSchema alike. Under Performed every block’s reader is the narrator, as under Narrator, and every line is made with its speaker’s performance note: a phrase of at most 60 characters, CADENCE_PHRASE_MAX, on how the narrator plays that character. Notes live on the audiobook book record beside reading, keyed by sheet id or by a name no sheet carries — the book’s, not the sheet’s, since another narrator plays Odile another way — and a speaker with no note is read plain. Narration takes no note. Under Performed, as under Cast, a run needs a current cast, since the note follows the line’s speaker. The note is rendered as the line’s phrase: a leading tag on the rows that take a phrase as a tag (ElevenLabs v3, Fish S2), an instruction on the rows that take one; the line’s own direction and markers render after it, and the whole rendered text is bounded by the reader’s cap as 146 bounds every block. A line is its own request, as every block is, so a note cannot run on into the narration after it — the reason this rides on the block split rather than on one long request. A narrator whose row takes no phrase cannot perform: the Voices panel says so on each noted speaker, note · not on this reader, in warning, and the door says it before anything is made, as a missing voice is said; the lines are then read plain, and the take records that the note was not applied. The take’s direction hash includes the note, so changing a speaker’s note makes every line of theirs stale across the book, counted on the row (4 lines · 2 stale). In Voices, under Performed, a speaker row is name and count over the note field, 28 high with its character count; the focused row adds Hear <name> and Sent as. Hear Odile renders the selected line when it is hers, else her first line in the chapter, with the note, as a voice preview — cached, never a take, priced on the button when the reader is cloud. Arke may propose notes from the sheets, one card for the cast, accepted whole or discarded; accepting writes the book record and nothing else.

Binding — a narrator for the book. 146 made the narrator the app’s (turn 70), so changing it for one book changed every read in the app. This amends it: the audiobook book record gains narrator, absent by default — the app’s narrator, followed as it changes — or a voice chosen for this book, resolved by narratorVoice as every narrator is, a clone bound to its world. Settings › General stays the app default and every other read keeps using it. The picker opens from the Narration row in Voices and from the narrator on the door’s voices row, which today links to Settings: a 580px dialog titled Narrator over the book’s data line, a seg App narrator · George or This book, the voices in 48 rows — a play button, name over reader, price as data, a tick — and the selected voice tried on the selected block with its direction rendered for that reader, as a voice preview: cached, never a take. Before Use for this book the dialog states what the switch does, as data rows: the blocks that go stale across the book, the direction the new reader cannot express, the price of reading the book again as Read the book would price it, and the old narrator’s takes, kept. Nothing is made by the press; the next read makes the stale blocks and is priced as any read is. Direction the new reader cannot express — a delivery, a marker, a performance note — is held, not dropped: kept on the record, left out of the rendered text, drawn struck in the view ([whispered] through a line), and counted (38 of 51 markers held). This amends 146’s re-check, which dropped it; a held control never reaches the reader, so it never flags a block, and it comes back when a reader that can express it returns. Takes follow the reader: a take is current for a block when its reader, text and direction match the block’s now, so switching back to George makes his kept takes current again without a call, and a block with a current take for the new reader is made. Takes are never deleted by a switch.

Binding — sizes and copy. The workspace keeps 126’s columns — rail 46, centre 983, manuscript 640, side 250, dock 331. Blocks: speaker column 96, text at var(--text-md)/1.75, marks cell 44, box-sizing:border-box. Filter chips are 24 high with the count in mono. The chip, the filter and the Voices dot share one colour per speaker. On-screen copy is labels and data — awaiting recording, 2 words differ, no line id — with no caption under any control.

Binding · turn 155 The voiced story — every block marked with who reads it, the speaker corrected by hand, a take recorded by a person as well as made by a voice, markers that direct the reading inside a block, a narrator who performs the cast, and a narrator chosen for the book (story mode; extends 146b and 130a; amends 130’s cast and 146’s mark column and states)

Binding — the margin is the speaker. In the Audiobook view the 70px mark column of 146b becomes a 96px speaker column holding a chip: an 8px dot and the name in var(--type-label), 22px high, ellipsed. The chip names who speaks the block by the cast — under Narrator as under Cast, since who speaks is the prose’s fact and who reads is the Voices panel’s. Narration and the title are narrator in --neutral-400; a speaker with a sheet takes a colour; a name no sheet carries is a dashed dot in --muted-foreground. A line’s block carries a 2px rule and a 7% tint in its speaker’s colour; narration carries neither, so the lines stand out of the prose without a label. Colours are a new token set, --voice-1 to --voice-6, one pair for light and one for dark, given to the book’s speakers in the order of their first line in the book and repeated past six, so a speaker keeps one colour in every chapter; the narrator never takes one, and --success, --warning and --destructive are never a speaker’s, since the state dot uses them. Beside the state dot a 44px marks cell shows how the kept take was made: a waveform for a voice, a microphone for a recording, nothing when there is no take. The row over the blocks is a filter — Everyone, Narrator, then each speaker in colour order, each with its block or line count — and choosing one dims every other block to 40% and makes Play play that speaker’s made takes alone (Odile Sarn · 2 of 4); the choice is not kept past the page.

Binding — the cast is derived, and a correction outlives it. 130 made the cast of lines derived and never authored; this amends it. The record at productions/<production>/.voices/<chapter>.json gains pins: authored corrections kept beside the derived lines, each { paragraph, quote, occurrence, speaker } where speaker is a sheet id, a name no sheet carries, or narration — this span is not a line. A press on a block’s chip opens the speaker menu, 236px: a search, IN THIS CHAPTER with Narration first and the chapter’s speakers, then CAST with the rest of the world’s sheets, each with its voice as data (no voice); a name typed that no sheet carries is offered as itself. Words selected inside a narration block open the same menu for the selection and make it a line: the selection must sit in one paragraph, cross no line, and hold between 1 and 600 characters, 130’s cap; otherwise the menu does not open. A pin is verified as a derived line is — the quote found exactly once at its occurrence in its paragraph, whitespace folded — and applied over the derived lines: a derived line that overlaps a pin gives way. Cast again keeps every pin that still verifies and derives around it; a pin whose words have moved is dropped and counted in the stamp (1 correction lost), never re-placed by guess. A pinned block carries a pin in its marks cell; the stamp counts pins (cast · v4 · 10 lines · 1 set by you). A pin changes who reads the block, so a take made for the old speaker goes stale by 146’s rule. A pin is written through the cast record’s ownership-checked path; it touches no sheet, no world track and no gate. The cast of a chapter with pins is current exactly as before: against the version and the hash of the prose.

Binding — a take is made or recorded. 146’s take gains a source: made, as before, or recorded, an audio file the author brings. Upload sits in the block’s Takes, and a file dropped on a block opens the same dialog, 540px: the block’s words in its speaker’s colour, the file with its waveform and technical line, the checks, the performer and the rights, Keep as take. WAV, FLAC, MP3 and M4A are read, one file a block, up to 10 minutes and 200 MB; the file is prepared through the audio foundation’s local path (issue 117) to the take format, 44.1 kHz mono, and no byte of it leaves the machine. The checks are the foundation’s QC report shown as data: loudness, peak and noise floor against Retail’s figures, and the words — a local transcript compared with the block’s text, match, 2 words differ, or words · unchecked where no local transcriber is present. A warning never refuses: a take with a noisy floor is kept and says so, and Retail export treats it as a take it must bring to profile. A hard incompatibility — undecodable, silent, over the limits — refuses in one clause on the file. Rights is required once a dialog, My voice · Authorized · Licensed, recorded as an AudioRightsEvent acknowledgement with a new scope recorded-take (an amendment to AudioRightsScopeSchema); the performer is the event’s performerRef, user-only, never in logs or a provider payload. A recorded take is production media as a made one is: a file under artifacts/ with a sidecar naming the chapter, paragraph and occurrence, the text hash, the source file’s hash and the prepared hash, the QC report and the acknowledgement id; its cost is nothing. It is chosen on the record as any take is, and it is current while the block’s text hash matches — a change of reader or of direction does not stale a recording, since neither made it; changed words do. A block whose chosen take is a current recording is never remade by Read the chapter or Read the book.

Binding — a speaker can be recorded. In the Voices panel a row is two lines, name and count over the reader, and each reader is a menu: the sheet’s voice, as 146 draws it, or Recorded, with an optional performer. Recorded is the book’s choice, kept on the audiobook book record beside reading as a list of sheet ids and narrator — an author may record their own narration — and never on the sheet, whose voice stays the voice every other read uses. Under Cast a recorded speaker’s block is made only by a recording: with no current recorded take it is awaiting, a fifth state beside 146’s four — the hollow dot with a microphone in the marks cell — counted in the foot and on the door’s row and voices (Odile Sarn · recorded · 2 awaiting). Rows are file, line, check, in a 38 band; what passes or warns is ticked, what is refused is not and cannot be; the rights are given once for the batch.   • Issue 1330 builds 165c over 155h: a search that takes focus and matches every word against the name, provider, reader and attributes; All · This machine · Cloud with counts, Saved only once the world has a saved voice; the list grouped with this machine first; rows named Kokoro · this machine, never mistral · voxtral-mini-tts; arrows, Enter and Space in the list; the switch's costs as rows beside the chosen voice, and Use for this book waiting for them.
  • Drift: the Reader seg (Flash · Flash-Lite) waits for 1329; Hear on the chosen voice is one button rather than the drawn quote of the block.
Binding · turn 165 The audiobook read by Gemini — the head and the block panel the build lost, a narrator found by search, sounds among the markers, voices designed and replicated for the book, the book quoted, stopped and picked up again, a saved voice out of reach, and the book out on this machine (story mode; extends t146 and t155; amends 155e’s head and block panel and 155h’s list)

Binding — planned controls are absent, not disabled. A control whose service has not landed is not in the build: no struck Sound chip waiting for 1334, no greyed Design a voice waiting for 1332, no Saved filter with nothing behind it. It appears when the coordinator reports the capability behind it — a reader that declares sounds, a provider that can design, a voice library that holds saved voices — so the structure ships once and each issue turns its controls on by reporting what it can do. A disabled control with no way to enable it is the prototype’s dead affordance, and the house does not ship one. What this turn builds now: the head, the block panel, the searchable narrator dialog with the switch’s costs, provider names, and the widths below.

Binding — the head names the reading. The chapter’s view row is 155e’s: the Manuscript · Audiobook seg, then the reading as a menu button in mono — Performed · Charon, the reading in --muted-foreground and the narrator in the foreground, a chevron — then Play and Read the chapter · N blocks · $X at the right. Play is there whenever one block has a made take and gives way to Stop and Skip while it plays; the priced read is the primary while anything is left to make. The menu, 248, is headed READING · WHOLE BOOK: Narrator, Performed, Cast as radio items with their data (one voice, notes, 7 voices), a rule, and Narrator…, which opens 165c. A choice here writes the book’s reading exactly as the door’s seg does, and is refused while a run is going as that seg is. This is the chapter’s way into Performed; the build had none.

Binding — the block panel is words, chips and one row of buttons. The title is Block 16 · Odile Sarn in --type-label semibold, sentence case, with no tracking — not two columns of letter-spaced capitals — and under it one mono line naming the reader by its voice and role: read by Charon · narrator, · performed under Performed, read by Anna · Maren Kest under Cast. Delivery is six pill chips 24 high that wrap, the chosen one filled, a radiogroup named Delivery; what the reader cannot do is struck with the reason as the title. The marker list shows a plate and the words it covers verbatim — the span as the block has it, never wrapped in quotation marks of its own, so “Whoever cut the tenth key, cannot become ““Whoever cut the tenth key,””; a point names its neighbour, before and the words. Under it the add buttons — Marker · Pause · Breath · Emphasis, and Sound when 1334 reports it — each a 24-high dashed pill holding a plus and one word that never part (white-space: nowrap); the row wraps between buttons, never inside one. Each is named for what it adds (Add pause). A take row is v2 · 0:04 · George · Kokoro: the version, the running time, the voice and the reader’s name from the catalogue.

Binding — a provider is a name and a place, never an id. Every audiobook surface names a reader by the catalogue’s words: the provider’s display name and where it runs — Kokoro · this machine, Google · cloud, Mistral · cloud — and, where a model is the reader, the reader’s name (Gemini Flash, Eleven v3, Voxtral). mistral · voxtral-mini-tts is an id and is never on screen: not in the dialog’s rows, the Voices panel, the door’s chips, the take rows, the confirm press or the price sheet. An id the catalogue cannot name shows the provider’s display name alone.

Binding — the model belongs to the reader. 146 refused a model on every block and this turn keeps it: Gemini Flash or Flash-Lite is part of the reader, chosen where the voice is chosen — the narrator dialog’s Reader seg (165c), a sheet’s Voice page — and only shown elsewhere: in Voices, on the door’s chips, on a take. No block, marker, run or dock prompt chooses a model. Changing Flash for Flash-Lite is a change of reader with the same costs stated before the press, and the same takes kept. Flash is offered first for a new cloud choice; Flash-Lite is chosen, never fallen back to. An existing character keeps the voice it has: nothing here recasts anyone.

Binding — a narrator found by search. 155h’s dialog becomes 165c: 860 by 640, two columns under the seg. The left, 400: a search that takes focus on open and matches the voice’s name, its provider’s name, its attributes and language, with the matches counted in it (14 of 343); chips All · This machine · Saved · Cloud with counts, a radiogroup; then the list, a listbox, in groups under 28-high bands — ON THIS MACHINE first, SAVED FOR THIS WORLD next, CLOUD last, each by provider and then name. A local voice is never below a cloud one and never behind a scroll the chips cannot reach, so the free voices stay found. Rows are 155h’s, 48 high — Hear <name>, the name over Provider · where · words, the price as data, the tick — with a grey rule on the current narrator and the foreground rule and tick on the choice. The right: the chosen voice and its Reader seg, Hear on the selected block with the block’s direction rendered and what the reader cannot do struck, then the costs as 155h states them — blocks stale, direction held, the book’s read price, the old narrator’s takes kept — asked of the coordinator on every pick and shown as … until answered; Use for this book waits for the answer. Arrow keys move in the list, Enter chooses, Space plays, Escape closes and focus returns to the button that opened it.

Binding — sounds are markers at a point. Planned with 1334. A sound is the third kind of marker, beside a delivery over a span and a cue at a point: a vocal event — laughs, sighs, gasps, clears throat, coughs, chuckles, the set a reader’s row declares — placed at a point in the block’s text and kept on the audiobook record as every marker is; the prose never holds one. On the page it is its word in brackets in italic mono on an outline, [sighs], where a delivery sits on a filled plate. The marker menu (165b) adds SOUND after CUE; a reader that cannot make a sound has the group struck and one clause under it (Kokoro reads measured or urgent · no sounds). A sound the new reader cannot make is held on a switch as 155h holds a delivery, counted with the markers, and sent again when a reader that can returns.

Binding — voices made for the book. Planned with 1332 and 1333. A speaker’s reader menu in Voices, and the Voice tab of a sheet, gain Design a voice… and Replicate a voice… when the provider reports it can. Designing (165d) starts from the sheet’s words, which may be edited here and are never written back; one of the speaker’s lines is the test; the press makes three candidates at a price stated on it, each a preview and never a take; Keep candidate N saves one voice to the world under a name and assigns it, and the candidates not kept are gone when the dialog closes. Replicating (165e) takes a reference and a consent statement in the same voice, checks both as a take is checked, shows the service’s same-speaker answer as data, and records the rights and performer once; nothing is created, and nothing is spent, until both pass. A kept voice is listed under SAVED FOR THIS WORLD with its origin (from Odile’s sheet) or its expiry (expires 3 Oct).

Binding — the book quoted, read, stopped and picked up. Planned with 1328 and 1335. Read the book (165h) states, for a reader billed by the token, the tokens in and out as an estimate, the notes counted in them, the recorded speakers left out, the blocks already made and not charged again, the rates with the date they were taken, and where the words go; one figure is on the press. While it runs (165f) the head says where it is in blocks and in money spent against the quote and Stop takes the primary’s place; each row carries its own state. After a stop (165g) the head says what was kept and spent, and the press is Read the rest, priced for what is missing alone; a request sent and not answered before the stop is counted as spent and never sent again.

Binding — a saved voice out of reach says so before a run. Planned with 1331. A saved voice is bound to the provider project that made it. When the key in Settings belongs to another project, or a replicated voice has expired, the voice is not in this project or expired in warning on its Voices row and the door’s chip, before any run, as no voice · narrator already is; its lines are not read in another voice without that being said. A press opens 165i: where it was saved, the key now, what it reads, and three ways back — the right key, the same words designed again as a new voice with its lines stale, or another voice — each with what it costs.

Binding — export needs this machine and nothing else. Planned with 1336, which finishes 146d. The sheet (165j) exports the chosen take of every block of every whole chapter, counts the rest with its dashed door, and says in one line what it needs: this machine · no provider · no key. A book read in the cloud exports with no credential present.

Binding — widths. At 1360 the workspace is 126’s. When the centre is narrower than the blocks’ 640, the gap and the side, the side keeps 250 and the blocks give up width, to 460; the gap and the centre’s padding fall to 20. At 1200 × 790 with the dock (165k) the centre is 823 and the blocks 513: the block panel sits beside them, on screen, and while a block is chosen the side holds its panel alone, the Voices group one press away on the head’s narrator. The filter keeps the chips that fit and counts the rest (+1). The side goes under the blocks only when the centre is under 700, and there the chapter is one column (165l): the view seg and Play, then the reading and the priced read, the filter as a row that swipes, the speaker’s name over a line rather than in a margin, and the block panel as a sheet raised by a press on a block, every target 44. The narrator dialog below 700 is a full-height sheet (165m) in one column.

Binding — keyboard, focus and names. The reading button is a menu button (aria-haspopup, aria-expanded) over a menu of radio items; the delivery chips a radiogroup; the add buttons buttons, named; the voices a listbox of options with aria-selected; each play named Hear <name>; a block’s state dot says its state in words to a screen reader, not in colour alone. Dialogs and sheets hold focus and give it back. Nothing here animates under prefers-reduced-motion but the play state.

The counting of bells

ManuscriptAudiobookPerformed· CharonPlayRead the chapter · 4 blocks · $0.05
Everyone31Narrator21Maren Kest5Odile Sarn4+1
narratorOdile did not let go of her hand. The bell had stopped; the water had not.
Odile Sarn[whispered]“Whoever cut the tenth key,” she said, [sighs]“cut it for this.”
narratorShe said it to the rope, not to Maren,[pause]and Maren let it stand there between them.
Maren Kest[laughs][breaking]“You shouldn’t.”
narrator[warm]Below them the tide came in all at once, the way it did when it had been waiting.
narratorNeither of them counted the bells after that. [breath]Somewhere under the Vigil, very low, something began again.

A sound is the third kind of marker, beside a delivery over a span and a cue at a point: a vocal event — laughs, sighs, gasps, clears throat, coughs, chuckles, the set a reader’s row declares — placed at a point in the block’s text and kept on the audiobook record as every marker is; the prose never holds one. On the page it is its word in brackets in italic mono on an outline, [sighs], where a delivery sits on a filled plate. The marker menu (165b) adds SOUND after CUE; a reader that cannot make a sound has the group struck and one clause under it (Kokoro reads measured or urgent · no sounds). A sound the new reader cannot make is held on a switch as 155h holds a delivery, counted with the markers, and sent again when a reader that can returns.

Binding — voices made for the book. Planned with 1332 and 1333. A speaker’s reader menu in Voices, and the Voice tab of a sheet, gain Design a voice… and Replicate a voice… when the provider reports it can. Designing (165d) starts from the sheet’s words, which may be edited here and are never written back; one of the speaker’s lines is the test; the press makes three candidates at a price stated on it, each a preview and never a take; Keep candidate N saves one voice to the world under a name and assigns it, and the candidates not kept are gone when the dialog closes. Replicating (165e) takes a reference and a consent statement in the same voice, checks both as a take is checked, shows the service’s same-speaker answer as data, and records the rights and performer once; nothing is created, and nothing is spent, until both pass. A kept voice is listed under SAVED FOR THIS WORLD with its origin (from Odile’s sheet) or its expiry (expires 3 Oct).

Binding — the book quoted, read, stopped and picked up. Planned with 1328 and 1335. Read the book (165h) states, for a reader billed by the token, the tokens in and out as an estimate, the notes counted in them, the recorded speakers left out, the blocks already made and not charged again, the rates with the date they were taken, and where the words go; one figure is on the press. While it runs (165f) the head says where it is in blocks and in money spent against the quote and Stop takes the primary’s place; each row carries its own state. After a stop (165g) the head says what was kept and spent, and the press is Read the rest, priced for what is missing alone; a request sent and not answered before the stop is counted as spent and never sent again.

Binding — a saved voice out of reach says so before a run. Planned with 1331. A saved voice is bound to the provider project that made it. When the key in Settings belongs to another project, or a replicated voice has expired, the voice is not in this project or expired in warning on its Voices row and the door’s chip, before any run, as no voice · narrator already is; its lines are not read in another voice without that being said. A press opens 165i: where it was saved, the key now, what it reads, and three ways back — the right key, the same words designed again as a new voice with its lines stale, or another voice — each with what it costs.

Binding — export needs this machine and nothing else. Planned with 1336, which finishes 146d. The sheet (165j) exports the chosen take of every block of every whole chapter, counts the rest with its dashed door, and says in one line what it needs: this machine · no provider · no key. A book read in the cloud exports with no credential present.

Binding — widths. At 1360 the workspace is 126’s. When the centre is narrower than the blocks’ 640, the gap and the side, the side keeps 250 and the blocks give up width, to 460; the gap and the centre’s padding fall to 20. At 1200 × 790 with the dock (165k) the centre is 823 and the blocks 513: the block panel sits beside them, on screen, and while a block is chosen the side holds its panel alone, the Voices group one press away on the head’s narrator. The filter keeps the chips that fit and counts the rest (+1). The side goes under the blocks only when the centre is under 700, and there the chapter is one column (165l): the view seg and Play, then the reading and the priced read, the filter as a row that swipes, the speaker’s name over a line rather than in a margin, and the block panel as a sheet raised by a press on a block, every target 44. The narrator dialog below 700 is a full-height sheet (165m) in one column.

Binding — keyboard, focus and names. The reading button is a menu button (aria-haspopup, aria-expanded) over a menu of radio items; the delivery chips a radiogroup; the add buttons buttons, named; the voices a listbox of options with aria-selected; each play named Hear <name>; a block’s state dot says its state in words to a screen reader, not in colour alone. Dialogs and sheets hold focus and give it back. Nothing here animates under prefers-reduced-motion but the play state.
